Endorsement: California isn’t a lab rat. Prop 40 treats us like one
There’s no denying the visceral satisfaction of a billionaire bloodletting. But will the measure’s wealth tax actually help the state?
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:42 p.m.
Taxation, like everything else in life, is an exercise in trade-offs.
How much public good can a tax extract before it passes the tipping point into harm?
As it relates to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php) on California’s November ballot, many believe you don’t have to look very hard to find where the cost-benefit needle falls.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on anyone whose total net worth is greater than $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, and who was a California resident on Jan. 1, 2026. After administrative costs, 90% of the revenue would go to public healthcare, while the other 10% would go to food assistance and education. The total collected could range from $28 billion to $100 billion — depending on whose math you believe. (California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the state will “probably” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) collect “tens of billions.”)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Whatever the total, there’s no denying that California billionaires — who by some counts control a combined $2 trillion (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) in wealth — can afford to shoulder it.
Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and a coauthor of Prop 40, called the measure a “rounding error” on the fortunes of California’s wealthiest.
For this mostly bloodless toll, Californians get relief from President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful” Medicaid cuts and radiate with satisfaction at sending a landmark message about wealth inequality.
Or so it would seem.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Is Prop 40 so flawlessly executed that California has nothing to lose if it passes?
Opposition from the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood, California Medical Association, the NAACP, California Professional Firefighters and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California suggests not.
Let’s start with the healthcare organizations, which would effectively receive 90% of Prop 40’s funds. Why are they opposed?
Dustin Corcoran, CEO of the California Medical Association, said in an endorsement interview that there’s no guarantee Prop 40’s payload will arrive in time to backfill Trump’s cuts. The state has no existing system for assessing billionaire wealth, he said, and it will likely take years to develop one.
Corcoran cited his experience as a backer of Prop 56, which passed in 2016 and imposed a tax on vape products.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It probably took the Franchise Tax Board 10 years of us beating them up because they couldn’t figure out how to get the tax right,” he said. “And that was a fairly straightforward thing to try and figure out.”
Even if the money does land, and that’s a big if, Corcoran argued that weak “anti-supplantation” protections in the measure will allow lawmakers to spend its revenue however they see fit — undermining one of Prop 40’s most powerful arguments, the urgency of the moment for healthcare.
University of Missouri School of Law Professor David Gamage, one of Prop 40’s coauthors, disputed these notions. He estimated that “75% of billionaire wealth is in publicly traded assets,” making much of it easy to track. And even if the measure does have supplantation holes, political pressure will prevent California politicians from treating Prop 40 revenue like a slush fund.
These vague assurances don’t persuade Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Healthcare organizations like hers, she said, use forward-looking budgets. They can’t commit to providing services if they can’t definitively rely on money coming in to pay for them.
Meanwhile, Prop 40 puts the money Hicks can count on in jeopardy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because California’s budget is overly dependent on income taxes — roughly half of which (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7)historically come from the ultra-wealthy top 1% of taxpayers.
Studying the impacts of Prop 40 “was an eye-opening experience for what California’s tax structure is and how the wealthy are a part of it,” Hicks said.
This gets at the real questions surrounding Prop 40 and why so many otherwise progressive organizations oppose the tax: Will billionaires leave the state if the measure passes, and will they take their companies with them?
“Good riddance” is the popular retort among online commentators.
But that attitude is childish and self-defeating. A recent case study explained why.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, left California in 2020, citing high taxes as one of his reasons. He took Tesla’s corporate headquarters with him to Texas the following year.
By some estimates, California lost an estimated $2.5 billion (https://www.businessinsider.com/why-did-elon-musk-move-texas-wealth-tax-capital-gains-2021-11) in capital gains revenue from one stock transaction in the first year of Musk’s move. In a state where 40% of state dollars are required by law to go to public education, that’s a $1 billion hole in California’s school budget from one man alone.
This answers why the formidable California Teachers Association — never one to shy away from a back-alley tax brawl — doesn’t support Prop 40.
Then there are the jobs.
Many Tesla workers stayed behind in California. But new Tesla jobs are now sprouting up across Texas, including nearly 10,000 for a proposed $10 billion solar cell factory (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/09/18/teslas-10-1-billion-texas-solar-gigafactory-clears-key-tax-hurdle/).
You’ve heard the aphorism, “Keep your friends close and your enemies closer.” Here’s a real-world example of why.
Sending billionaires and the jobs and economic might that come with them to Texas or Florida does not help California. Nor does it help the prospects for building a more just society. It simply makes those red states more powerful.
So, will Prop 40 send billionaires fleeing?
A working paper from Stanford says yes, (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) and argues that exodus will result in a net tax revenue loss of nearly $39 billion for California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Indeed, some billionaires — most famously Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has dumped hundreds of millions into opposing Prop 40 — have already announced their departures.
Some economists dispute the Stanford study (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988796082176375), arguing it ignores basic human motivation. Prop 40 will hit any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. Why would they uproot their lives now over a one-time tax they have to pay regardless — especially one they can easily afford?
We’d counter that California’s nation-leading 13.3% marginal income tax rate — necessary as it may be (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php), given our state’s finances — already poses a flight risk. Even Gamage said he was “uncomfortable” (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) with the top rate. A wealth tax merely compounds a danger that already exists.
It’s true that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has committed to ponying up (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/billionaires-fight-tax-hike-jensen-160907521.html) his estimated $8 billion in dues. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has apparently agreed to stay in California for eight years after strong-arming the company (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php#:~:text=Meta%20revealed%20in%20a%20Securities%20and%20Exchange%20Commission%20filing%20that%20Mark%20Zuckerberg%20was%20considering%20leaving%20California%2C%20but%20agreed%20to%20stay%20after%20the%20company%20gave%20him%20a%20new%20stock%20deal) into eating his wealth tax burden.
Yet the debate around flight risk has largely focused on the wealthiest of the wealthy. Less discussed are the paper billionaires — those with unrealized stakes in valuable startups and other private companies.
Prop 40’s method for assessing this wealth (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan) is dubious. Some believe the measure allows voting shares or control percentage to be used in calculating wealth, rather than ownership stake, which could be wildly off. The measure does offer a mechanism for the wealthy to contest their asset valuations, but at what point are companies going to decide enough is enough and seek their fortunes elsewhere?
“Only idiot startup founders stay in Cali” if Prop 40 passes, billionaire investor Mark Cuban has said on social media. (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan?utm_source=chatgpt.com) “You can bet if I’m investing in a multi-billion-dollar startup, I’m asking them to move from California first.”
“Boo hoo,” you say?
California’s startup culture is a crucial engine of its economy. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, companies in the state receive nearly half of all American venture capital (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2024/4942/CalFacts-2024-120224.pdf). Another study found these investments help employ 1.2 million people (https://www.nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/California-VC-State-Data.pdf). As companies grow their roots, California’s budget sees the benefit.
Many argue that the talent ecosystem in California makes an exodus impossible.
But people said the same thing about Hollywood for decades. Now the entertainment industry is shedding thousands of jobs to states like Georgia and North Carolina that offer more favorable economic incentives.
If movie titans are willing to abandon a company town practically built to indulge their excess, it’s not a stretch to imagine a significant portion of the tech universe fleeing to Miami or Austin, where workforce housing is cheaper, they would pay no state income tax, and the sword of future wealth taxes would no longer hang over their endeavors.
All this speaks to why tackling extreme wealth is better approached at the federal level. There’s evidence from Spain and elsewhere that the wealthy will shop around regionally (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to) for lower taxes. There’s much less evidence that they’ll flee the country.
We are already seeing momentum for a federal inequality crackdown. Democrats are poised to retake Congress, and Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Burbank, recently announced legislation that would impose an excise tax of 23.8% (https://news.bgov.com/bloomberg-government-news/house-democrat-pitches-new-wealth-tax-as-midterms-draw-near) on most line-of-credit loans — which are leveraged against assets like stocks — above $1 million.
Ever wonder how the Zuckerbergs of the world get by on a salary of $1? Borrowing against stock gives them access to cash without having to pay capital gains. In fact, in some cases, interest payments on these loans are tax deductible under federal policy.
Fixing these loopholes would force the ultra-wealthy to either take salaries or liquidate assets when they need cash, which would mean income tax boons for states like California.
Obviously, with Trump still in charge, it could take a few years for these and other changes to manifest.
Instead of being patient, however, Prop 40 throws the full weight of risk on California’s shoulders now.
“Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?”
We wholeheartedly agree with these sentiments, espoused by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders at a recent rally in support of Prop 40.
But living up to them demands strategic thinking, not primal screaming.
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be.
Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tLQFHYqkVtY)
It just happens to be one dropped into the maw of the world’s fourth-largest economy — a wealthy state in aggregate, but one with a volatile, incoherent system of taxation (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php) and the highest poverty rate in the nation.
If Prop 40 backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. Our sales and income taxes are already the highest in the nation; there’s no more room for hikes. Meanwhile, Prop 13 stunts our ability to raise new revenue from property taxes.
No one is coming to save us. And it won’t be the wealthy who suffer.
Maybe, just maybe, the stakes are too high in California to be playing a game of chicken. Maybe the brightest and boldest minds in the field of economic justice should help stabilize California’s tax base before turning our state into a laboratory?

content.text:
Response to “The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act” March
4, 2026
Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), Emmanuel
Saez (UC Berkeley), Darien Shanske (UC Davis)
March 17, 2026
This report responds to the study by Rauh et al. (2026) published on March 4, 2026 that
purports to examine the fiscal consequences of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act
(CBTA) ballot initiative (full text here) and to criticize our expert report.
Rauh et al.’s analysis and conclusions simply do not rest on an estimate of the CBTA as
written. The CBTA is a one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax, payable over five years and
so roughly equivalent to a 1% annual tax assessed for only five years plus an
interest-deferral charge. Yet Rauh et al. estimate taxpayer mobility responses as
though taxpayers face a recurring 5% annual wealth tax as a permanent ongoing
tax. Their revenue estimate of that policy also depends on a crucial and highly unlikely
assumption: they count the income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in
perpetuity because of this large recurrent 5% annual tax as a cost but on the
revenue side, they assume that the wealth tax applies only once. This
unreasonable asymmetry is the largest flaw in their analysis.
On top of this, the Rauh et al. analysis is also based on incorrect claims about California
law and about who counts as a California resident for tax law purposes. There is no
real evidence that any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for
California at the end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA under the legal standard that will
actually apply. Below we elaborate as to the specific issues.
Analyzing an imaginary permanent 5% wealth tax
The CBTA is a one-time tax on the net wealth of California billionaires. The rate
is 5%, but individuals can elect to spread payment over five years, yielding an annual
burden of 1% per year, plus an interest charge. We estimate that this tax raises $100
billion with comparatively very modest reductions in California income tax revenue.
In contrast, Rauh et al. (2026) estimate the mobility effects of a permanent and
annual 5% tax on billionaire wealth (using behavioral elasticities from the empirical
literature on mobility responses to wealth taxes). On the cost side, they count the
income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in perpetuity but on the revenue side, they
assume that the wealth tax applies only once. Yet if the tax were permanent then surely
the revenue it would raise should be included, which would of course add hundreds of
billions of dollars in revenue. To emphasize, the Rauh et al. estimate depends on the
assumption that the costs of the tax will last forever, but the revenues will be one time
only.
By way of apparent justification for analyzing a different policy than the one that
is actually in the CBTA, Rauh et al. appear to argue that some taxpayers may assume
that the wealth tax would be permanent (and ongoing with a 5% annual rate assessed
every year). They do not explain the basis for that assumption. Under a standard model
of rational expectations, taxpayers’ behavioral responses are tied to expectations with
quick corrections if these expectations are not met. If the wealth tax turned out not to be
permanent, then surely the model should reflect some updating of taxpayer
assumptions. If the CBTA is not followed by another wealth tax, taxpayers will have no
reason to act as though the CBTA is permanent and the Rauh et al. projections would
grossly overstate taxpayers’ behavioral responses.
Put another way, we think it is highly unlikely that taxpayers would act as though
a tax were permanent unless that tax were, in fact, permanent. If so, then a serious
estimate of the revenue effect of the tax should include those permanent future
revenues. Yet Rauh et al. appear to assume that the supposedly permanent tax they
analyze will not collect a single dollar of revenue in future years. (This could only be true
if every single billionaire left California in the first year and with no new taxpayers
becoming billionaires in California thereafter, but there is absolutely no justification for
assuming or concluding this from Rauh et al.’s analysis, in addition to this being
completely implausible).
Although Rauh et al.’s assumptions are implausible, the underlying notion that
either the introduction or passage of the CBTA might affect expectations as to future
policy is plausible and would be worth analyzing with a serious methodology. Such an
analysis would be inherently speculative, and should thus be considered along with
other speculative possible effects of the CBTA, both positive and negative, such as
potential effects as to combating harms resulting from rising inequality. Most importantly,
such an analysis should also include estimates of the economic effects of the CBTA’s
revenues being used to address California’s expected health care crisis. Regardless,
even if it might be plausible to speculate that either the introduction or the passage of
the CBTA might increase expectations as to the likelihood of a future wealth tax, it is not
plausible to assess this as though taxpayers would expect a guaranteed future tax at
five times the effective annual rate of the CBTA enacted immediately and sustained
permanently. Further, even under their assumptions on mobility responses, a 5%
recurrent annual tax would raise much more revenue than what is lost through income
tax losses (see below).
Further, the enactment of the CBTA has no legal effect on the ability of the
California legislature or the voters to enact a subsequent wealth tax. If voters believe
that the legislature or the voters are likely to adopt additional wealth taxes in the future,
then they should already hold those beliefs and the CBTA should have only at most
modest incremental effects on those expectations.
Most critically, there is no plausible justification for assuming that taxpayers
would expect a 5% annual tax, rather than the roughly 1% annual tax imposed by the
CBTA. Even if somehow the CBTA made a future tax more likely, and if that future tax
were for some reason the exact same as the CBTA, then voters should expect a 1%
annual tax rate.
This is a point worth emphasizing again: almost the entirety of the Rauh et al.
analysis rests on the assumption that voters treat the CBTA as informative of the
likelihood of a future wealth tax, but their supposed analysis offers no explanation for
why that future wealth tax would be a 5% annual tax. Why wouldn’t the future tax rate
voters expect be .4% (the cap currently in the California Constitution)? Or 1%, the
effective rate in the CBTA? If it were, their estimates would be vastly different.
As a result of this mix and match methodology and series of hidden and
undefended assumptions, including counting losses as permanent and using their 1.5%
discount rate, the annual income tax loss is magnified by a factor 67 - almost two orders
of magnitude. This explains the negative net present value they find.1
Incorrect assumption that substantial movement has already occurred
Rauh et al. also significantly undercount the revenue potential of the CBTA
because they assume that “[n]early 30% of the Act’s wealth tax base has already
departed.” This high number is based on press reports about billionaires claiming that
they have taken steps to try to change their residency either before January 1, 2026 (6
billionaires listed in their Table 6) or after January 1, 2026 and up to early March (4
additional billionaires listed in their Table 7). These assumptions misunderstand both the
CBTA and California residency law. Buying real estate, opening office space out of
state, or announcing a move is not the same as successfully severing California tax
residence which requires, as a matter of law, uprooting most of the individual’s personal
and business ties to California.
If voters approve the CBTA, it will fall on any billionaire who was a California
resident as of January 1, 2026. Residence for purposes of the CBTA is based on
1 Rauh et al. (2026) state that “The net present value of the Act is −$24.7 billion.” That is, they say the
present value of permanently lost income tax revenue more than offsets the one-time wealth tax
collections. For a sense of how improbable that number is, consider that using the elasticity they employ
to reach that conclusion, the revenue-maximizing permanent annual wealth tax rate would be nearly 10%.
(Elasticity roughly refers to how much taxpayers are likely to respond to a tax). Formally, the revenue
maximizing rate for a permanent wealth tax is given by the inverse of the semi-elasticity which Rauh et al.
assume to be around 10 (see Boll, Saez, and Zucman 2026 for details).
longstanding residence rules under California’s personal income tax. Among other
aspects of this approach, which is almost a century old, California residents are
presumed to remain in California until they are able to demonstrate that their absence
from California was not temporary. When California courts make that determination,
they look to whether a person’s closest personal, business, family, and political ties are
to California, or instead to somewhere else, Thus, simply buying real estate, opening
office space out of state, or announcing a planned move is not the same as successfully
severing California tax residence. As courts recognize, it is very easy to claim to move,
but very hard to actually do it. Many Californians have claimed to have “moved” for tax
purposes, only to find that their move was not effective (at least not as early as they
hoped).
Given that the CBTA is a one-time tax in 2026, there is an obvious and powerful
incentive for a potential taxpayer to take up, or claim that they have taken up, a
temporary abode somewhere else. Billionaires already own, and can readily purchase,
new vacation homes elsewhere, and that will be obvious to courts. In light of the
obvious incentives and opportunities for billionaires to misrepresent their residency
plans, the close attention California tax authorities can give to each of the two hundred
or so CBTA taxpayers, and the inherent difficulty of resettling deep personal, business,
and other ties in such a short period, it is unlikely that many billionaires have actually
taken the steps necessary to establish a change of residency as a matter of law. An
analysis by experts in California residency tax planning legal services explains this in
persuasive detail.2
Put another way, little in the current public record offers real reason to think that
any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for California at the
end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA. Certainly we see no evidence to suggest that
individuals who now say they are spending time elsewhere will remain outside the state,
rather than, say, returning to Silicon Valley in January of 2027. At best, Rauh et al. offer
a kind of worst-case scenario for the CBTA’s revenue; we do not believe that presenting
only the worst case is a reasonable way to project the CBTA’s effects.
Finally, from press reports and direct discussions, some billionaires apparently
initially misunderstood the text of the initiative and thought they would be taxed based
on their voting share in their business rather than the economic value of their share. As
a result, many, including the Google founders Larry Page and Sergei Brin, incorrectly
thought their tax liability would be much more than the 5% tax. We hope that this issue
has now been cleared up (see our explanation) and that billionaires now understand
that the tax will never exceed 5% of the economic value of their wealth. If this was
2 Rauh et al. argue that billionaires who cannot establish residency by January 1 elsewhere may be
hoping that the January 1, 2026 date will be eventually struck down as unconstitutional. This is an unlikely
scenario, as we have explained in depth elsewhere. In short, the current residency rule is longstanding in
California and other states, and the Supreme Court has since the Nineteenth Century repeatedly
approved tax laws that extend back to the beginning of the calendar year or further.
indeed a pivotal reason for wanting to leave, it is possible that some billionaires who
announced their intent to depart will revisit their decision, especially as it also becomes
clear, as we argue above, that these paper moves were not likely effective anyway.
Smaller Points
California income tax paid by billionaires. Rauh et al. (2026) estimate that California
billionaires pay $4.55 billion (in their central scenario) or about .24% of their wealth in
annual California income tax in 2025 while we estimate that they pay around $3 billion
per year. This moderate size discrepancy arises primarily because they assume that the
212 billionaires have reported individual income equal to 78% of the highest 212 income
earners. We assume, based on direct evidence from Balkir et al. (2025) matching US
wide billionaires to income tax data, that billionaires’ income is only 50% of the reported
income of the highest income earners.3 This discrepancy however is relatively modest
(compared to the scoring issues discussed above).
Rauh et al. (2026) also assume that the California income tax loss due to
billionaires leaving is proportional to their wealth with Google founders Larry Page,
Sergei Brin, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg accounting for slightly over 90% of
the wealth that has left (in both their shortlist in Table 6 and their longer list in Table 7).
Using public filings on stock sales, executive compensation, and dividends paid out,
Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) find that the California centi-billionaires pay a much
lower California income tax (relative to their wealth) than mere California billionaires
overall. In particular, they find that Page, Brin, and Zuckerberg paid only $269 million4 in
California income tax between the three of them in 2025, which is only .04% of their
wealth in 2025, much less than the .24% of wealth paid by “ordinary” California
billionaires overall estimated by Rauh et al. (2026). As a result, even if these 3
centibillionaires have or will depart California, something we very much doubt, the
consequences for California income tax collections are almost negligible ($269 million is
about .2% of the $120 billion expected total California income taxes collected in 2025).
Is Larry Ellison a California resident? Forbes listed Larry Ellison, whose wealth at the
end of 2025 was $245 billion, slightly over 10% of total CA billionaire wealth, as a
California resident up to Jan 10, 2026, at which point Forbes started listing him as a
Florida resident. Forbes had also listed him as a Hawaii resident for a couple of years
during COVID. Rauh et al. (2026) argue that he left California years ago. The reality is
that California residency for tax purposes is not public information and hence we cannot
know for sure. We followed the Forbes list which is based on careful investigative
reporting but we recognize that it is possible that Larry Ellison, who had already taken
4 Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) provide those estimates annually. On average from 2019 to 2025, Brin,
Page, and Zuckerberg paid only $222 million per year in California income taxes.
3 This 50% number is also what comes out when analyzing Survey of Consumer Finance data that
provides information on both reported income and wealth for a representative sample of very high
wealth/high income families (see Saez and Zucman 2019, p. 466).
steps to move out of California well before the billionaire tax initiative, may not be a
resident by January 1, 2026, and hence not liable for the tax.
Conversely, it is likely that Forbes misses some California billionaires as well,
either heirs of old fortunes who are not as visible as they tend to have diversified wealth
or new billionaires who haven’t yet attracted public attention. For example, the Wall
Street Journal listed 255 California billionaires in 2024 when Forbes listed only 196.
Non US-citizens California residents. Both Rauh et al. (2026) and our report failed to
include the California billionaires who are not US-citizens but liable for California income
(or wealth) tax as residents.5 Most of them are very long-term residents of California.
There are 24 of them at the end of 2025 with a total wealth of $110 billion, about 5% of
the total, that should be included in the revenue estimates, an omission we will correct
in our next iteration.
Concluding Points
Rauh et al. can reach their extreme conclusions only through a series of
improbable assumptions and misunderstandings large and small. Taken on its own
terms, the policy they analyze (which is not, on any set of reasonable assumptions, the
effects of the actual CBTA) would raise hundreds of billions of dollars. Our prior analysis
as well as nonpartisan analysis by California’s Legislative Analyst's Office each
conclude those policies would on net raise tens of billions to offset California’s
health-care funding crisis.

residents. This explains why many users of the Forbes data (including ourselves) fail to include non-US
citizens in their analysis.

Response to “The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act” March
4, 2026
Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), Emmanuel
Saez (UC Berkeley), Darien Shanske (UC Davis)
March 17, 2026
This report responds to the study by Rauh et al. (2026) published on March 4, 2026 that
purports to examine the fiscal consequences of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act
(CBTA) ballot initiative (full text here) and to criticize our expert report.
Rauh et al.’s analysis and conclusions simply do not rest on an estimate of the CBTA as
written. The CBTA is a one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax, payable over five years and
so roughly equivalent to a 1% annual tax assessed for only five years plus an
interest-deferral charge. Yet Rauh et al. estimate taxpayer mobility responses as
though taxpayers face a recurring 5% annual wealth tax as a permanent ongoing
tax. Their revenue estimate of that policy also depends on a crucial and highly unlikely
assumption: they count the income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in
perpetuity because of this large recurrent 5% annual tax as a cost but on the
revenue side, they assume that the wealth tax applies only once. This
unreasonable asymmetry is the largest flaw in their analysis.
On top of this, the Rauh et al. analysis is also based on incorrect claims about California
law and about who counts as a California resident for tax law purposes. There is no
real evidence that any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for
California at the end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA under the legal standard that will
actually apply. Below we elaborate as to the specific issues.
Analyzing an imaginary permanent 5% wealth tax
The CBTA is a one-time tax on the net wealth of California billionaires. The rate
is 5%, but individuals can elect to spread payment over five years, yielding an annual
burden of 1% per year, plus an interest charge. We estimate that this tax raises $100
billion with comparatively very modest reductions in California income tax revenue.
In contrast, Rauh et al. (2026) estimate the mobility effects of a permanent and
annual 5% tax on billionaire wealth (using behavioral elasticities from the empirical
literature on mobility responses to wealth taxes). On the cost side, they count the
income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in perpetuity but on the revenue side, they
assume that the wealth tax applies only once. Yet if the tax were permanent then surely
the revenue it would raise should be included, which would of course add hundreds of
billions of dollars in revenue. To emphasize, the Rauh et al. estimate depends on the
assumption that the costs of the tax will last forever, but the revenues will be one time
only.
By way of apparent justification for analyzing a different policy than the one that
is actually in the CBTA, Rauh et al. appear to argue that some taxpayers may assume
that the wealth tax would be permanent (and ongoing with a 5% annual rate assessed
every year). They do not explain the basis for that assumption. Under a standard model
of rational expectations, taxpayers’ behavioral responses are tied to expectations with
quick corrections if these expectations are not met. If the wealth tax turned out not to be
permanent, then surely the model should reflect some updating of taxpayer
assumptions. If the CBTA is not followed by another wealth tax, taxpayers will have no
reason to act as though the CBTA is permanent and the Rauh et al. projections would
grossly overstate taxpayers’ behavioral responses.
Put another way, we think it is highly unlikely that taxpayers would act as though
a tax were permanent unless that tax were, in fact, permanent. If so, then a serious
estimate of the revenue effect of the tax should include those permanent future
revenues. Yet Rauh et al. appear to assume that the supposedly permanent tax they
analyze will not collect a single dollar of revenue in future years. (This could only be true
if every single billionaire left California in the first year and with no new taxpayers
becoming billionaires in California thereafter, but there is absolutely no justification for
assuming or concluding this from Rauh et al.’s analysis, in addition to this being
completely implausible).
Although Rauh et al.’s assumptions are implausible, the underlying notion that
either the introduction or passage of the CBTA might affect expectations as to future
policy is plausible and would be worth analyzing with a serious methodology. Such an
analysis would be inherently speculative, and should thus be considered along with
other speculative possible effects of the CBTA, both positive and negative, such as
potential effects as to combating harms resulting from rising inequality. Most importantly,
such an analysis should also include estimates of the economic effects of the CBTA’s
revenues being used to address California’s expected health care crisis. Regardless,
even if it might be plausible to speculate that either the introduction or the passage of
the CBTA might increase expectations as to the likelihood of a future wealth tax, it is not
plausible to assess this as though taxpayers would expect a guaranteed future tax at
five times the effective annual rate of the CBTA enacted immediately and sustained
permanently. Further, even under their assumptions on mobility responses, a 5%
recurrent annual tax would raise much more revenue than what is lost through income
tax losses (see below).
Further, the enactment of the CBTA has no legal effect on the ability of the
California legislature or the voters to enact a subsequent wealth tax. If voters believe
that the legislature or the voters are likely to adopt additional wealth taxes in the future,
then they should already hold those beliefs and the CBTA should have only at most
modest incremental effects on those expectations.
Most critically, there is no plausible justification for assuming that taxpayers
would expect a 5% annual tax, rather than the roughly 1% annual tax imposed by the
CBTA. Even if somehow the CBTA made a future tax more likely, and if that future tax
were for some reason the exact same as the CBTA, then voters should expect a 1%
annual tax rate.
This is a point worth emphasizing again: almost the entirety of the Rauh et al.
analysis rests on the assumption that voters treat the CBTA as informative of the
likelihood of a future wealth tax, but their supposed analysis offers no explanation for
why that future wealth tax would be a 5% annual tax. Why wouldn’t the future tax rate
voters expect be .4% (the cap currently in the California Constitution)? Or 1%, the
effective rate in the CBTA? If it were, their estimates would be vastly different.
As a result of this mix and match methodology and series of hidden and
undefended assumptions, including counting losses as permanent and using their 1.5%
discount rate, the annual income tax loss is magnified by a factor 67 - almost two orders
of magnitude. This explains the negative net present value they find.1
Incorrect assumption that substantial movement has already occurred
Rauh et al. also significantly undercount the revenue potential of the CBTA
because they assume that “[n]early 30% of the Act’s wealth tax base has already
departed.” This high number is based on press reports about billionaires claiming that
they have taken steps to try to change their residency either before January 1, 2026 (6
billionaires listed in their Table 6) or after January 1, 2026 and up to early March (4
additional billionaires listed in their Table 7). These assumptions misunderstand both the
CBTA and California residency law. Buying real estate, opening office space out of
state, or announcing a move is not the same as successfully severing California tax
residence which requires, as a matter of law, uprooting most of the individual’s personal
and business ties to California.
If voters approve the CBTA, it will fall on any billionaire who was a California
resident as of January 1, 2026. Residence for purposes of the CBTA is based on

to reach that conclusion, the revenue-maximizing permanent annual wealth tax rate would be nearly 10%.
(Elasticity roughly refers to how much taxpayers are likely to respond to a tax). Formally, the revenue

aspects of this approach, which is almost a century old, California residents are
presumed to remain in California until they are able to demonstrate that their absence
from California was not temporary. When California courts make that determination,
they look to whether a person’s closest personal, business, family, and political ties are
to California, or instead to somewhere else, Thus, simply buying real estate, opening
office space out of state, or announcing a planned move is not the same as successfully
severing California tax residence. As courts recognize, it is very easy to claim to move,
but very hard to actually do it. Many Californians have claimed to have “moved” for tax
purposes, only to find that their move was not effective (at least not as early as they
hoped).
Given that the CBTA is a one-time tax in 2026, there is an obvious and powerful
incentive for a potential taxpayer to take up, or claim that they have taken up, a
temporary abode somewhere else. Billionaires already own, and can readily purchase,
new vacation homes elsewhere, and that will be obvious to courts. In light of the
obvious incentives and opportunities for billionaires to misrepresent their residency
plans, the close attention California tax authorities can give to each of the two hundred
or so CBTA taxpayers, and the inherent difficulty of resettling deep personal, business,
and other ties in such a short period, it is unlikely that many billionaires have actually
taken the steps necessary to establish a change of residency as a matter of law. An
analysis by experts in California residency tax planning legal services explains this in
persuasive detail.2
Put another way, little in the current public record offers real reason to think that
any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for California at the
end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA. Certainly we see no evidence to suggest that
individuals who now say they are spending time elsewhere will remain outside the state,
rather than, say, returning to Silicon Valley in January of 2027. At best, Rauh et al. offer
a kind of worst-case scenario for the CBTA’s revenue; we do not believe that presenting
only the worst case is a reasonable way to project the CBTA’s effects.
Finally, from press reports and direct discussions, some billionaires apparently
initially misunderstood the text of the initiative and thought they would be taxed based
on their voting share in their business rather than the economic value of their share. As
a result, many, including the Google founders Larry Page and Sergei Brin, incorrectly
thought their tax liability would be much more than the 5% tax. We hope that this issue
has now been cleared up (see our explanation) and that billionaires now understand
that the tax will never exceed 5% of the economic value of their wealth. If this was

Smaller Points
California income tax paid by billionaires. Rauh et al. (2026) estimate that California
billionaires pay $4.55 billion (in their central scenario) or about .24% of their wealth in
annual California income tax in 2025 while we estimate that they pay around $3 billion
per year. This moderate size discrepancy arises primarily because they assume that the
212 billionaires have reported individual income equal to 78% of the highest 212 income
earners. We assume, based on direct evidence from Balkir et al. (2025) matching US
wide billionaires to income tax data, that billionaires’ income is only 50% of the reported
income of the highest income earners.3 This discrepancy however is relatively modest
(compared to the scoring issues discussed above).
Rauh et al. (2026) also assume that the California income tax loss due to
billionaires leaving is proportional to their wealth with Google founders Larry Page,
Sergei Brin, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg accounting for slightly over 90% of
the wealth that has left (in both their shortlist in Table 6 and their longer list in Table 7).
Using public filings on stock sales, executive compensation, and dividends paid out,
Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) find that the California centi-billionaires pay a much
lower California income tax (relative to their wealth) than mere California billionaires
overall. In particular, they find that Page, Brin, and Zuckerberg paid only $269 million4 in
California income tax between the three of them in 2025, which is only .04% of their
wealth in 2025, much less than the .24% of wealth paid by “ordinary” California
billionaires overall estimated by Rauh et al. (2026). As a result, even if these 3
centibillionaires have or will depart California, something we very much doubt, the
consequences for California income tax collections are almost negligible ($269 million is
about .2% of the $120 billion expected total California income taxes collected in 2025).

Conversely, it is likely that Forbes misses some California billionaires as well,
either heirs of old fortunes who are not as visible as they tend to have diversified wealth
or new billionaires who haven’t yet attracted public attention. For example, the Wall
Street Journal listed 255 California billionaires in 2024 when Forbes listed only 196.
Non US-citizens California residents. Both Rauh et al. (2026) and our report failed to
include the California billionaires who are not US-citizens but liable for California income
(or wealth) tax as residents.5 Most of them are very long-term residents of California.
There are 24 of them at the end of 2025 with a total wealth of $110 billion, about 5% of
the total, that should be included in the revenue estimates, an omission we will correct
in our next iteration.
Concluding Points
Rauh et al. can reach their extreme conclusions only through a series of
improbable assumptions and misunderstandings large and small. Taken on its own
terms, the policy they analyze (which is not, on any set of reasonable assumptions, the
effects of the actual CBTA) would raise hundreds of billions of dollars. Our prior analysis
as well as nonpartisan analysis by California’s Legislative Analyst's Office each
conclude those policies would on net raise tens of billions to offset California’s
health-care funding crisis.

residents. This explains why many users of the Forbes data (including ourselves) fail to include non-US
citizens in their analysis.

Response to “The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act” March
4, 2026
Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), Emmanuel
Saez (UC Berkeley), Darien Shanske (UC Davis)
March 17, 2026
This report responds to the study by Rauh et al. (2026) published on March 4, 2026 that
purports to examine the fiscal consequences of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act
(CBTA) ballot initiative (full text here) and to criticize our expert report.
Rauh et al.’s analysis and conclusions simply do not rest on an estimate of the CBTA as
written. The CBTA is a one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax, payable over five years and
so roughly equivalent to a 1% annual tax assessed for only five years plus an
interest-deferral charge. Yet Rauh et al. estimate taxpayer mobility responses as
though taxpayers face a recurring 5% annual wealth tax as a permanent ongoing
tax. Their revenue estimate of that policy also depends on a crucial and highly unlikely
assumption: they count the income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in
perpetuity because of this large recurrent 5% annual tax as a cost but on the
revenue side, they assume that the wealth tax applies only once. This
unreasonable asymmetry is the largest flaw in their analysis.
On top of this, the Rauh et al. analysis is also based on incorrect claims about California
law and about who counts as a California resident for tax law purposes. There is no
real evidence that any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for
California at the end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA under the legal standard that will
actually apply. Below we elaborate as to the specific issues.
Analyzing an imaginary permanent 5% wealth tax
The CBTA is a one-time tax on the net wealth of California billionaires. The rate
is 5%, but individuals can elect to spread payment over five years, yielding an annual
burden of 1% per year, plus an interest charge. We estimate that this tax raises $100
billion with comparatively very modest reductions in California income tax revenue.
In contrast, Rauh et al. (2026) estimate the mobility effects of a permanent and
annual 5% tax on billionaire wealth (using behavioral elasticities from the empirical
literature on mobility responses to wealth taxes). On the cost side, they count the
income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in perpetuity but on the revenue side, they
assume that the wealth tax applies only once. Yet if the tax were permanent then surely
the revenue it would raise should be included, which would of course add hundreds of
billions of dollars in revenue. To emphasize, the Rauh et al. estimate depends on the
assumption that the costs of the tax will last forever, but the revenues will be one time
only.
By way of apparent justification for analyzing a different policy than the one that
is actually in the CBTA, Rauh et al. appear to argue that some taxpayers may assume
that the wealth tax would be permanent (and ongoing with a 5% annual rate assessed
every year). They do not explain the basis for that assumption. Under a standard model
of rational expectations, taxpayers’ behavioral responses are tied to expectations with
quick corrections if these expectations are not met. If the wealth tax turned out not to be
permanent, then surely the model should reflect some updating of taxpayer
assumptions. If the CBTA is not followed by another wealth tax, taxpayers will have no
reason to act as though the CBTA is permanent and the Rauh et al. projections would
grossly overstate taxpayers’ behavioral responses.
Put another way, we think it is highly unlikely that taxpayers would act as though
a tax were permanent unless that tax were, in fact, permanent. If so, then a serious
estimate of the revenue effect of the tax should include those permanent future
revenues. Yet Rauh et al. appear to assume that the supposedly permanent tax they
analyze will not collect a single dollar of revenue in future years. (This could only be true
if every single billionaire left California in the first year and with no new taxpayers
becoming billionaires in California thereafter, but there is absolutely no justification for
assuming or concluding this from Rauh et al.’s analysis, in addition to this being
completely implausible).
Although Rauh et al.’s assumptions are implausible, the underlying notion that
either the introduction or passage of the CBTA might affect expectations as to future
policy is plausible and would be worth analyzing with a serious methodology. Such an
analysis would be inherently speculative, and should thus be considered along with
other speculative possible effects of the CBTA, both positive and negative, such as
potential effects as to combating harms resulting from rising inequality. Most importantly,
such an analysis should also include estimates of the economic effects of the CBTA’s
revenues being used to address California’s expected health care crisis. Regardless,
even if it might be plausible to speculate that either the introduction or the passage of
the CBTA might increase expectations as to the likelihood of a future wealth tax, it is not
plausible to assess this as though taxpayers would expect a guaranteed future tax at
five times the effective annual rate of the CBTA enacted immediately and sustained
permanently. Further, even under their assumptions on mobility responses, a 5%
recurrent annual tax would raise much more revenue than what is lost through income
tax losses (see below).
Further, the enactment of the CBTA has no legal effect on the ability of the
California legislature or the voters to enact a subsequent wealth tax. If voters believe
that the legislature or the voters are likely to adopt additional wealth taxes in the future,
then they should already hold those beliefs and the CBTA should have only at most
modest incremental effects on those expectations.
Most critically, there is no plausible justification for assuming that taxpayers
would expect a 5% annual tax, rather than the roughly 1% annual tax imposed by the
CBTA. Even if somehow the CBTA made a future tax more likely, and if that future tax
were for some reason the exact same as the CBTA, then voters should expect a 1%
annual tax rate.
This is a point worth emphasizing again: almost the entirety of the Rauh et al.
analysis rests on the assumption that voters treat the CBTA as informative of the
likelihood of a future wealth tax, but their supposed analysis offers no explanation for
why that future wealth tax would be a 5% annual tax. Why wouldn’t the future tax rate
voters expect be .4% (the cap currently in the California Constitution)? Or 1%, the
effective rate in the CBTA? If it were, their estimates would be vastly different.
As a result of this mix and match methodology and series of hidden and
undefended assumptions, including counting losses as permanent and using their 1.5%
discount rate, the annual income tax loss is magnified by a factor 67 - almost two orders
of magnitude. This explains the negative net present value they find.1
Incorrect assumption that substantial movement has already occurred
Rauh et al. also significantly undercount the revenue potential of the CBTA
because they assume that “[n]early 30% of the Act’s wealth tax base has already
departed.” This high number is based on press reports about billionaires claiming that
they have taken steps to try to change their residency either before January 1, 2026 (6
billionaires listed in their Table 6) or after January 1, 2026 and up to early March (4
additional billionaires listed in their Table 7). These assumptions misunderstand both the
CBTA and California residency law. Buying real estate, opening office space out of
state, or announcing a move is not the same as successfully severing California tax
residence which requires, as a matter of law, uprooting most of the individual’s personal
and business ties to California.
If voters approve the CBTA, it will fall on any billionaire who was a California
resident as of January 1, 2026. Residence for purposes of the CBTA is based on
1 Rauh et al. (2026) state that “The net present value of the Act is −$24.7 billion.” That is, they say the
present value of permanently lost income tax revenue more than offsets the one-time wealth tax
collections. For a sense of how improbable that number is, consider that using the elasticity they employ
to reach that conclusion, the revenue-maximizing permanent annual wealth tax rate would be nearly 10%.
(Elasticity roughly refers to how much taxpayers are likely to respond to a tax). Formally, the revenue
maximizing rate for a permanent wealth tax is given by the inverse of the semi-elasticity which Rauh et al.
assume to be around 10 (see Boll, Saez, and Zucman 2026 for details).
longstanding residence rules under California’s personal income tax. Among other
aspects of this approach, which is almost a century old, California residents are
presumed to remain in California until they are able to demonstrate that their absence
from California was not temporary. When California courts make that determination,
they look to whether a person’s closest personal, business, family, and political ties are
to California, or instead to somewhere else, Thus, simply buying real estate, opening
office space out of state, or announcing a planned move is not the same as successfully
severing California tax residence. As courts recognize, it is very easy to claim to move,
but very hard to actually do it. Many Californians have claimed to have “moved” for tax
purposes, only to find that their move was not effective (at least not as early as they
hoped).
Given that the CBTA is a one-time tax in 2026, there is an obvious and powerful
incentive for a potential taxpayer to take up, or claim that they have taken up, a
temporary abode somewhere else. Billionaires already own, and can readily purchase,
new vacation homes elsewhere, and that will be obvious to courts. In light of the
obvious incentives and opportunities for billionaires to misrepresent their residency
plans, the close attention California tax authorities can give to each of the two hundred

and other ties in such a short period, it is unlikely that many billionaires have actually
taken the steps necessary to establish a change of residency as a matter of law. An

Put another way, little in the current public record offers real reason to think that
any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for California at the
end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA. Certainly we see no evidence to suggest that
individuals who now say they are spending time elsewhere will remain outside the state,
rather than, say, returning to Silicon Valley in January of 2027. At best, Rauh et al. offer
a kind of worst-case scenario for the CBTA’s revenue; we do not believe that presenting

initially misunderstood the text of the initiative and thought they would be taxed based
on their voting share in their business rather than the economic value of their share. As
a result, many, including the Google founders Larry Page and Sergei Brin, incorrectly
thought their tax liability would be much more than the 5% tax. We hope that this issue
has now been cleared up (see our explanation) and that billionaires now understand
that the tax will never exceed 5% of the economic value of their wealth. If this was

Their letter framed the California vote as potentially bigger than a single state measure.
"If the state that houses some of the country's most powerful billionaires votes to tax their wealth, it will kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states – and eventually at the federal level and in other countries," the signers wrote.
...
The letter said the measure would bring in about $100 billion, money that could help soften 2025 cuts to Medicaid and food assistance tied to President Donald Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Economists and advocates argue that taxing extreme wealth could help shore up public services while reducing billionaires' growing influence over elections and policy.

Response to “The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act” March
4, 2026
Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), Emmanuel
Saez (UC Berkeley), Darien Shanske (UC Davis)
March 17, 2026
This report responds to the study by Rauh et al. (2026) published on March 4, 2026 that
purports to examine the fiscal consequences of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act
(CBTA) ballot initiative (full text here) and to criticize our expert report.
Rauh et al.’s analysis and conclusions simply do not rest on an estimate of the CBTA as
written. The CBTA is a one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax, payable over five years and
so roughly equivalent to a 1% annual tax assessed for only five years plus an
interest-deferral charge. Yet Rauh et al. estimate taxpayer mobility responses as
though taxpayers face a recurring 5% annual wealth tax as a permanent ongoing
tax. Their revenue estimate of that policy also depends on a crucial and highly unlikely
assumption: they count the income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in
perpetuity because of this large recurrent 5% annual tax as a cost but on the
revenue side, they assume that the wealth tax applies only once. This
unreasonable asymmetry is the largest flaw in their analysis.
On top of this, the Rauh et al. analysis is also based on incorrect claims about California
law and about who counts as a California resident for tax law purposes. There is no
real evidence that any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for
California at the end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA under the legal standard that will
actually apply. Below we elaborate as to the specific issues.
Analyzing an imaginary permanent 5% wealth tax
The CBTA is a one-time tax on the net wealth of California billionaires. The rate
is 5%, but individuals can elect to spread payment over five years, yielding an annual
burden of 1% per year, plus an interest charge. We estimate that this tax raises $100
billion with comparatively very modest reductions in California income tax revenue.
In contrast, Rauh et al. (2026) estimate the mobility effects of a permanent and
annual 5% tax on billionaire wealth (using behavioral elasticities from the empirical
literature on mobility responses to wealth taxes). On the cost side, they count the
income tax loss due to billionaires leaving in perpetuity but on the revenue side, they
assume that the wealth tax applies only once. Yet if the tax were permanent then surely
the revenue it would raise should be included, which would of course add hundreds of
billions of dollars in revenue. To emphasize, the Rauh et al. estimate depends on the
assumption that the costs of the tax will last forever, but the revenues will be one time
only.
By way of apparent justification for analyzing a different policy than the one that
is actually in the CBTA, Rauh et al. appear to argue that some taxpayers may assume
that the wealth tax would be permanent (and ongoing with a 5% annual rate assessed
every year). They do not explain the basis for that assumption. Under a standard model
of rational expectations, taxpayers’ behavioral responses are tied to expectations with
quick corrections if these expectations are not met. If the wealth tax turned out not to be
permanent, then surely the model should reflect some updating of taxpayer
assumptions. If the CBTA is not followed by another wealth tax, taxpayers will have no
reason to act as though the CBTA is permanent and the Rauh et al. projections would
grossly overstate taxpayers’ behavioral responses.
Put another way, we think it is highly unlikely that taxpayers would act as though
a tax were permanent unless that tax were, in fact, permanent. If so, then a serious
estimate of the revenue effect of the tax should include those permanent future
revenues. Yet Rauh et al. appear to assume that the supposedly permanent tax they
analyze will not collect a single dollar of revenue in future years. (This could only be true
if every single billionaire left California in the first year and with no new taxpayers
becoming billionaires in California thereafter, but there is absolutely no justification for
assuming or concluding this from Rauh et al.’s analysis, in addition to this being
completely implausible).
Although Rauh et al.’s assumptions are implausible, the underlying notion that
either the introduction or passage of the CBTA might affect expectations as to future
policy is plausible and would be worth analyzing with a serious methodology. Such an
analysis would be inherently speculative, and should thus be considered along with
other speculative possible effects of the CBTA, both positive and negative, such as
potential effects as to combating harms resulting from rising inequality. Most importantly,
such an analysis should also include estimates of the economic effects of the CBTA’s
revenues being used to address California’s expected health care crisis. Regardless,
even if it might be plausible to speculate that either the introduction or the passage of
the CBTA might increase expectations as to the likelihood of a future wealth tax, it is not
plausible to assess this as though taxpayers would expect a guaranteed future tax at
five times the effective annual rate of the CBTA enacted immediately and sustained
permanently. Further, even under their assumptions on mobility responses, a 5%
recurrent annual tax would raise much more revenue than what is lost through income
tax losses (see below).
Further, the enactment of the CBTA has no legal effect on the ability of the
California legislature or the voters to enact a subsequent wealth tax. If voters believe
that the legislature or the voters are likely to adopt additional wealth taxes in the future,
then they should already hold those beliefs and the CBTA should have only at most
modest incremental effects on those expectations.
Most critically, there is no plausible justification for assuming that taxpayers
would expect a 5% annual tax, rather than the roughly 1% annual tax imposed by the
CBTA. Even if somehow the CBTA made a future tax more likely, and if that future tax
were for some reason the exact same as the CBTA, then voters should expect a 1%
annual tax rate.
This is a point worth emphasizing again: almost the entirety of the Rauh et al.
analysis rests on the assumption that voters treat the CBTA as informative of the
likelihood of a future wealth tax, but their supposed analysis offers no explanation for
why that future wealth tax would be a 5% annual tax. Why wouldn’t the future tax rate
voters expect be .4% (the cap currently in the California Constitution)? Or 1%, the
effective rate in the CBTA? If it were, their estimates would be vastly different.
As a result of this mix and match methodology and series of hidden and
undefended assumptions, including counting losses as permanent and using their 1.5%
discount rate, the annual income tax loss is magnified by a factor 67 - almost two orders
of magnitude. This explains the negative net present value they find.1
Incorrect assumption that substantial movement has already occurred
Rauh et al. also significantly undercount the revenue potential of the CBTA
because they assume that “[n]early 30% of the Act’s wealth tax base has already
departed.” This high number is based on press reports about billionaires claiming that
they have taken steps to try to change their residency either before January 1, 2026 (6
billionaires listed in their Table 6) or after January 1, 2026 and up to early March (4
additional billionaires listed in their Table 7). These assumptions misunderstand both the
CBTA and California residency law. Buying real estate, opening office space out of
state, or announcing a move is not the same as successfully severing California tax
residence which requires, as a matter of law, uprooting most of the individual’s personal
and business ties to California.
If voters approve the CBTA, it will fall on any billionaire who was a California
resident as of January 1, 2026. Residence for purposes of the CBTA is based on
1 Rauh et al. (2026) state that “The net present value of the Act is −$24.7 billion.” That is, they say the
present value of permanently lost income tax revenue more than offsets the one-time wealth tax
collections. For a sense of how improbable that number is, consider that using the elasticity they employ
to reach that conclusion, the revenue-maximizing permanent annual wealth tax rate would be nearly 10%.
(Elasticity roughly refers to how much taxpayers are likely to respond to a tax). Formally, the revenue
maximizing rate for a permanent wealth tax is given by the inverse of the semi-elasticity which Rauh et al.
assume to be around 10 (see Boll, Saez, and Zucman 2026 for details).
longstanding residence rules under California’s personal income tax. Among other
aspects of this approach, which is almost a century old, California residents are
presumed to remain in California until they are able to demonstrate that their absence
from California was not temporary. When California courts make that determination,
they look to whether a person’s closest personal, business, family, and political ties are
to California, or instead to somewhere else, Thus, simply buying real estate, opening
office space out of state, or announcing a planned move is not the same as successfully
severing California tax residence. As courts recognize, it is very easy to claim to move,
but very hard to actually do it. Many Californians have claimed to have “moved” for tax
purposes, only to find that their move was not effective (at least not as early as they
hoped).
Given that the CBTA is a one-time tax in 2026, there is an obvious and powerful
incentive for a potential taxpayer to take up, or claim that they have taken up, a
temporary abode somewhere else. Billionaires already own, and can readily purchase,
new vacation homes elsewhere, and that will be obvious to courts. In light of the
obvious incentives and opportunities for billionaires to misrepresent their residency
plans, the close attention California tax authorities can give to each of the two hundred
or so CBTA taxpayers, and the inherent difficulty of resettling deep personal, business,
and other ties in such a short period, it is unlikely that many billionaires have actually
taken the steps necessary to establish a change of residency as a matter of law. An
analysis by experts in California residency tax planning legal services explains this in
persuasive detail.2
Put another way, little in the current public record offers real reason to think that
any significant number of individuals on the Forbes billionaire list for California at the
end of 2025 will avoid the CBTA. Certainly we see no evidence to suggest that
individuals who now say they are spending time elsewhere will remain outside the state,
rather than, say, returning to Silicon Valley in January of 2027. At best, Rauh et al. offer
a kind of worst-case scenario for the CBTA’s revenue; we do not believe that presenting
only the worst case is a reasonable way to project the CBTA’s effects.
Finally, from press reports and direct discussions, some billionaires apparently
initially misunderstood the text of the initiative and thought they would be taxed based
on their voting share in their business rather than the economic value of their share. As
a result, many, including the Google founders Larry Page and Sergei Brin, incorrectly
thought their tax liability would be much more than the 5% tax. We hope that this issue
has now been cleared up (see our explanation) and that billionaires now understand
that the tax will never exceed 5% of the economic value of their wealth. If this was
2 Rauh et al. argue that billionaires who cannot establish residency by January 1 elsewhere may be
hoping that the January 1, 2026 date will be eventually struck down as unconstitutional. This is an unlikely
scenario, as we have explained in depth elsewhere. In short, the current residency rule is longstanding in
California and other states, and the Supreme Court has since the Nineteenth Century repeatedly
approved tax laws that extend back to the beginning of the calendar year or further.
indeed a pivotal reason for wanting to leave, it is possible that some billionaires who
announced their intent to depart will revisit their decision, especially as it also becomes
clear, as we argue above, that these paper moves were not likely effective anyway.
Smaller Points
California income tax paid by billionaires. Rauh et al. (2026) estimate that California
billionaires pay $4.55 billion (in their central scenario) or about .24% of their wealth in
annual California income tax in 2025 while we estimate that they pay around $3 billion
per year. This moderate size discrepancy arises primarily because they assume that the
212 billionaires have reported individual income equal to 78% of the highest 212 income
earners. We assume, based on direct evidence from Balkir et al. (2025) matching US
wide billionaires to income tax data, that billionaires’ income is only 50% of the reported
income of the highest income earners.3 This discrepancy however is relatively modest
(compared to the scoring issues discussed above).
Rauh et al. (2026) also assume that the California income tax loss due to
billionaires leaving is proportional to their wealth with Google founders Larry Page,
Sergei Brin, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg accounting for slightly over 90% of
the wealth that has left (in both their shortlist in Table 6 and their longer list in Table 7).
Using public filings on stock sales, executive compensation, and dividends paid out,
Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) find that the California centi-billionaires pay a much
lower California income tax (relative to their wealth) than mere California billionaires
overall. In particular, they find that Page, Brin, and Zuckerberg paid only $269 million4 in
California income tax between the three of them in 2025, which is only .04% of their
wealth in 2025, much less than the .24% of wealth paid by “ordinary” California
billionaires overall estimated by Rauh et al. (2026). As a result, even if these 3
centibillionaires have or will depart California, something we very much doubt, the
consequences for California income tax collections are almost negligible ($269 million is
about .2% of the $120 billion expected total California income taxes collected in 2025).
Is Larry Ellison a California resident? Forbes listed Larry Ellison, whose wealth at the
end of 2025 was $245 billion, slightly over 10% of total CA billionaire wealth, as a
California resident up to Jan 10, 2026, at which point Forbes started listing him as a
Florida resident. Forbes had also listed him as a Hawaii resident for a couple of years
during COVID. Rauh et al. (2026) argue that he left California years ago. The reality is
that California residency for tax purposes is not public information and hence we cannot
know for sure. We followed the Forbes list which is based on careful investigative
reporting but we recognize that it is possible that Larry Ellison, who had already taken
4 Boll, Saez, and Zucman (2026) provide those estimates annually. On average from 2019 to 2025, Brin,
Page, and Zuckerberg paid only $222 million per year in California income taxes.
3 This 50% number is also what comes out when analyzing Survey of Consumer Finance data that
provides information on both reported income and wealth for a representative sample of very high
wealth/high income families (see Saez and Zucman 2019, p. 466).
steps to move out of California well before the billionaire tax initiative, may not be a
resident by January 1, 2026, and hence not liable for the tax.
Conversely, it is likely that Forbes misses some California billionaires as well,
either heirs of old fortunes who are not as visible as they tend to have diversified wealth
or new billionaires who haven’t yet attracted public attention. For example, the Wall
Street Journal listed 255 California billionaires in 2024 when Forbes listed only 196.
Non US-citizens California residents. Both Rauh et al. (2026) and our report failed to
include the California billionaires who are not US-citizens but liable for California income
(or wealth) tax as residents.5 Most of them are very long-term residents of California.
There are 24 of them at the end of 2025 with a total wealth of $110 billion, about 5% of
the total, that should be included in the revenue estimates, an omission we will correct
in our next iteration.
Concluding Points
Rauh et al. can reach their extreme conclusions only through a series of
improbable assumptions and misunderstandings large and small. Taken on its own
terms, the policy they analyze (which is not, on any set of reasonable assumptions, the
effects of the actual CBTA) would raise hundreds of billions of dollars. Our prior analysis
as well as nonpartisan analysis by California’s Legislative Analyst's Office each
conclude those policies would on net raise tens of billions to offset California’s
health-care funding crisis.
5 The Forbes data provides citizenship information but only state level residence for US and Chinese
residents. This explains why many users of the Forbes data (including ourselves) fail to include non-US
citizens in their analysis.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm weighing the key questions for the decision, starting with the revenue estimate. The LAO sees a temporary inflow of tens of billions against under $1B a year in ongoing costs, while proponents claim about $100B and Rauh puts the NPV at a loss of $25B to $39B. I'm working out what the LAO's figures imply for net present value, assuming a mid-range collection of $40-60B.

I'm checking how sensitive the LAO-implied net present value is to the ongoing loss and the discount rate, since even at their figures the result looks positive. I'm also weighing who would gain from the one-time revenue, like low-income Californians keeping Medi-Cal coverage, against the roughly 200 to 250 billionaires who would bear the tax.

I'm weighing the legal exposure next: the tax could be struck down in whole or part, and the retroactive residency date looks especially vulnerable, since someone who left in early 2026 would still be taxed on wealth as of late 2026. If a court moved that date past the election, anyone who already departed might escape the tax entirely.

I'm now looking at the precedent risk: passing the tax could push other wealthy people and startup founders to leave or avoid moving to California, and the proponents openly want it to set up further wealth taxes, which weakens the "one-time" framing that polls suggest most Californians already doubt. I'm also noting that the measure is effectively budgeted through the ballot by a single union, with only a weak guard against supplanting existing funding.

I'm now looking at how the union's role and its ties to the hospitals and Newsom bear on the measure, since the reported bargaining-chip angle could matter for judging motives even if it doesn't settle the merits. I'm also weighing the valuation question for private companies, particularly how control rights for founders with voting control might be treated.

I'm now looking at how the valuation rules could hit private startup founders, since a recent funding round might be used as a floor even though preferred-stock prices overstate what common shares are worth. That could push founders to pay more than 5% of their real economic value, which I see as a design flaw for the startup ecosystem, though the deferral option for illiquid taxpayers softens the liquidity problem.

Next I'll weigh the legal risk, checking how legal scholars view the constitutional challenges, and then look at the evidence on billionaire departures and the reported "Zuckerberg deal." After that I want the healthcare side, meaning the size and timing of the federal cuts, and a test of whether the LAO's "less than $1B" ongoing cost holds up. I'll also see where mainstream economists such as Furman, Summers, the Tax Policy Center, and the Hamilton Project land.

Next I'm going to check how legal scholars view the constitutional challenges, then look at the evidence on billionaire departures and the reported Zuckerberg deal. I'll also see how the prediction markets price the measure and whether the union's alleged bargaining-chip role holds up.
