I'm weighing the key questions for the decision, starting with the revenue estimate. The LAO sees a temporary inflow of tens of billions against under $1B a year in ongoing costs, while proponents claim about $100B and Rauh puts the NPV at a loss of $25B to $39B. I'm working out what the LAO's figures imply for net present value, assuming a mid-range collection of $40-60B.

I'm checking how sensitive the LAO-implied net present value is to the ongoing loss and the discount rate, since even at their figures the result looks positive. I'm also weighing who would gain from the one-time revenue, like low-income Californians keeping Medi-Cal coverage, against the roughly 200 to 250 billionaires who would bear the tax.

I'm weighing the legal exposure next: the tax could be struck down in whole or part, and the retroactive residency date looks especially vulnerable, since someone who left in early 2026 would still be taxed on wealth as of late 2026. If a court moved that date past the election, anyone who already departed might escape the tax entirely.

I'm now looking at the precedent risk: passing the tax could push other wealthy people and startup founders to leave or avoid moving to California, and the proponents openly want it to set up further wealth taxes, which weakens the "one-time" framing that polls suggest most Californians already doubt. I'm also noting that the measure is effectively budgeted through the ballot by a single union, with only a weak guard against supplanting existing funding.

I'm now looking at how the union's role and its ties to the hospitals and Newsom bear on the measure, since the reported bargaining-chip angle could matter for judging motives even if it doesn't settle the merits. I'm also weighing the valuation question for private companies, particularly how control rights for founders with voting control might be treated.

I'm now looking at how the valuation rules could hit private startup founders, since a recent funding round might be used as a floor even though preferred-stock prices overstate what common shares are worth. That could push founders to pay more than 5% of their real economic value, which I see as a design flaw for the startup ecosystem, though the deferral option for illiquid taxpayers softens the liquidity problem.

Next I'll weigh the legal risk, checking how legal scholars view the constitutional challenges, and then look at the evidence on billionaire departures and the reported "Zuckerberg deal." After that I want the healthcare side, meaning the size and timing of the federal cuts, and a test of whether the LAO's "less than $1B" ongoing cost holds up. I'll also see where mainstream economists such as Furman, Summers, the Tax Policy Center, and the Hamilton Project land.

Next I'm going to check how legal scholars view the constitutional challenges, then look at the evidence on billionaire departures and the reported Zuckerberg deal. I'll also see how the prediction markets price the measure and whether the union's alleged bargaining-chip role holds up.

Constitutional Flaws of California’s Proposed Wealth Tax
August 12, 2026 September 30, 2026 28 min read By: Jared Walczak (https://taxfoundation.org/about-us/staff/jared-walczak/) Download PDF (https://taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FF885_CA_Wealth_1.pdf)
Table of Contents
Key Findings
The California (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/) Billionaire Tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax/) A tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Act (Proposition 40), which imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ net worth, is vulnerable to numerous constitutional challenges, any of which could invalidate the tax in whole or in part.
Drafters’ characterization of the levy as an excise tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/excise-tax/) An excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. rather than a tax on property is irrelevant; if amendments superseding the state constitution’s limits on intangible property taxation fail, then the new tax fails as well.
The retroactive residency date is fatally flawed under Supreme Court precedent barring retroactive imposition of a “wholly new tax.”
The tax’s 100 percent apportionment (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/apportionment/) Apportionment is the determination of the percentage of a business’s profits subject to a given jurisdiction’s corporate income tax or other business tax. US states apportion business profits based on some combination of the percentage of company property, payroll, and sales located within their borders. system violates nexus, fair apportionment, and internal consistency requirements.
The measure’s sweeping anti-avoidance rules include assets the taxpayer does not own, raising due process issues and, in certain cases, guaranteeing double taxation (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/double-taxation/) Double taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. .
By seeking to lock taxpayers into full liability whether they stay or leave, the tax burdens the right to travel, which could force the state to defend these provisions under strict scrutiny.
The tax base (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax-base/) The tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. impermissibly includes US Treasuries and other federal obligations.
Uncapped penalties on appraisers who value hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns because they are grossly disproportionate to any good-faith errors.
Drafters have asked courts to reform the statute to cure any defects, but the measure’s constitutional flaws far exceed what can be accomplished through judicial reformation and point toward striking the tax down in its entirety.
Introduction
If California adopts a wealth tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/wealth-tax/) A wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary. , the only undisputed winners will be the lawyers. The California Billionaire Tax Act (CBTA), appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot as Proposition 40, is vulnerable to a range of legal challenges on numerous grounds and on multiple levels: as-applied challenges to the tax imposed on specific individuals; challenges to the validity of specific provisions as written, like the snapshot residency and valuation dates; and challenges to the constitutionality of the tax as a whole.
A prior paper examined how litigation over the CBTA’s residency and valuation provisions could require judicial reformation, eliminating some or all wealth tax liability for billionaires who leave the state in 2026—if the tax could survive such a challenge at all. [1] This paper explores the more fundamental question of whether the proposed wealth tax passes constitutional muster.
The measure’s drafters fully anticipated that their proposal would draw intense legal scrutiny and recognized that it would raise serious constitutional questions. They embedded a set of preemptive legal defenses into the tax’s design, attempting to insulate it from these challenges. But not all potential constitutional infirmities can be overcome by legal cunning, and the measure’s defensive provisions are an acknowledgment of a wealth tax’s fundamental legal vulnerabilities.
If courts invalidate the tax, California will have the worst of all worlds: a threat that drives away some of the state’s wealthiest taxpayers and spooks the next wave of startup founders, costly litigation that could drag on for years, and not a single dollar in new revenue. This is not a minor concern. The tax is legally dubious as well as economically damaging. This paper examines the legal deficiencies that could, and should, lead to the tax being struck down.
The Excise Tax Characterization Fails
The measure defines the wealth tax as an excise tax on the “activity” of “sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth.” [2] But courts, in California and at the federal level, have long held that the character of a tax is determined by its substance, not its form or label. [3] Merely calling a tax an excise tax does not make it one, and even if it is possible to define a tax as an excise in some fashion, it does not lose its ordinary characteristics.
A wealth tax is, fundamentally, a tax on property, and styling it as a tax on an “activity” does not change that fact, any more than ordinary real property taxes could be deemed to no longer be property taxes (and thus, perhaps, not subject to Proposition 13 assessment limits or rate caps) but rather an excise tax on the activity of sustaining ownership of real property. If excise tax framing can override the substance of a tax, that has implications for every taxpayer in California, because it could be used to avoid laws limiting any specific tax.
Fortunately, California and federal courts have historically disregarded labels when they conflict with the clear substance or nature of the tax in question, and it is a maxim of jurisprudence in California that “[t]he law respects form less than substance.” [4] The CBTA is a tax on both tangible and (especially) intangible property, with liability triggered by ownership on a fixed date, measured against net worth, and imposed without there being any transaction, transfer, or realization event. “Sustaining” accumulations of wealth is indistinguishable from ownership. The proposed wealth tax is a property tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/property-tax/) A property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. .
This matters because the state constitution imposes a 0.4 percent cap on the taxation of intangibles, and also requires taxes on property to be uniform, both of which undeniably conflict with the proposed wealth tax. [5] The measure’s drafters understood this, despite their efforts to frame the tax as an excise tax. They explicitly acknowledge the issue in one of their white papers on the proposal, [6] and their solution is to embed a constitutional amendment within the measure that authorizes this particular one-time tax notwithstanding any other provision of the constitution with which it might conflict.
Ballot measures are permitted to amend the constitution but not “revise” it—a distinction about how fundamental and sweeping the changes are. Some have suggested that the constitutional elements are broad enough to constitute an impermissible revision, and if courts came to that conclusion, then the state constitution’s limits on property taxation would apply to the tax, and its “excise tax” characterization is highly unlikely to save it. Similarly, courts may conclude that these constitutional amendments exceed what is permitted under the single subject rule for ballot initiatives, with the same result.
Meanwhile, the attempt to characterize the tax as an excise tax could backfire against proponents in federal constitutional litigation, because the whole framing of the tax is about taxing a status rather than a transaction or property ownership, which buttresses the case that this is a “wholly new tax”—a problem for its retroactivity, discussed below—and which complicates the tax’s already vexing apportionment problems.
The Retroactive Provisions Are Fatally Flawed
The CBTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who resided in California as of January 1, 2026, based on wealth measured on December 31, 2026. Since the measure is on the ballot in November, its residency snapshot predates the potential adoption of the tax by more than 10 months.
As noted in prior analyses, retroactivity is not necessarily a legal impediment by itself. Many taxes are modified retroactively in ways that have survived legal scrutiny. However, retroactivity has limits, some better defined than others. The period of retroactivity is a relevant consideration, but a period of less than a year is not unusual. Similarly, due process violations arise if “retroactive application is so harsh and oppressive as to transgress the constitutional limitation,” [7] which the courts would have to determine. Most pertinent for the wealth tax, however, is that the Supreme Court has distinguished between “modest” revisions of existing taxes and the adoption of a “wholly new tax,” [8] twice acting to strike down retroactive applications of a new tax—even when it only applied to periods when a taxpayer had good reason to believe that such a tax was forthcoming (“constructive notice”). [9]
The ordinary remedy for retroactivity is to exclusively apply the tax prospectively. Because the CBTA is designed as a one-time tax, however, this option is not readily available. The tax only contains one residency date, and it is retroactive. Invalidating any application prior to the November enactment date would therefore leave little, if any, of the tax intact.
Drafters knew the dates they chose invited such a challenge, and sought to build in a safety valve, asking courts to engage in “judicial reformation” to set later dates if these dates are deemed unconstitutional. The express request may help the case, but California’s courts have been reluctant to reform tax laws because they cannot reasonably anticipate whether lawmakers (or, in this case, voters) would have supported the measure had it been presented to them in revised form.
As the California appeals court noted in one such case, “In the context of cases involving tax statutes that violate the Commerce Clause, the courts have consistently declined to exercise the power of judicial reformation to cure the constitutional violation.” Rewriting a statute “would involve us in precisely the type of judicial policymaking and encroachment on the legislative function in violation of the separation of powers doctrine.” [10]

The Federal Facial Constitutionality of California’s Proposed Billionaire
Tax Act
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act (BTA) authorizes a facial constitutional challenge to its
provisions by any interested person within sixty days of voter approval through a validation
action that does not impose a tax-prepayment requirement.1 To prevail in this facial
constitutional challenge, the interested person must establish that the BTA always operates
unconstitutionally and that judicial enforcement is constitutionally barred under any
potential set of circumstances.2
Some opponents of the Act urge that the Act should be rejected by California voters
due to federal constitutional infirmities with the Act that would render it facially invalid in
such an action. We believe, similar to the attached litigation risk assessment by Gupta
Wessler LLP, that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial challenges.
None of the opponents’ federal constitutional claims support that the BTA is facially
unconstitutional.
Retroactivity under the Due Process Clause
The BTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires residing in
California as of January 1, 2026, based on their wealth valued as of December 31, 2026. The
BTA thus locks in tax liability before voter approval of the tax.
The Supreme Court has explained that such retroactive application of a tax statute is
constitutional when “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational
means.”3 This standard is exceptionally deferential; the judiciary does not adjudge the
wisdom and fairness of taxation because such economic policy determinations “remain
with the exclusive province of the legislative and executive branches.”4 All retroactive
economic laws, including tax legislation, trigger this same deferential judicial scrutiny.5
Retroactive tax laws are thus upheld under the Due Process Clause unless the retroactive
application bears no rational relationship to a permissible legislative purpose.
The BTA’s look-back mechanism for triggering its tax obligation readily survives this
minimal due-process threshold. The state’s legitimate purpose is to ensure that individuals

The BTA meets these Due Process and dormant Commerce Clause standards. To
start, the BTA would apply only to California residents as of the tax obligation date and would
be imposed on “net worth,” which is defined to exclude tangible property located outside of
the state.31 Residence therefore supplies the constitutional basis the Due Process Clause
requires, and the exclusion of out-of-state tangible property keeps the tax within the rule
described above.32
The BTA would also be apportioned in a constitutional manner. The tax apportions
100% of the tax base to California, but it also provides taxpayers with credits against the
resulting tax for taxes paid to other states on the same base. 33 That structure is no diZerent
from the structure that states use for purposes of their personal income taxes. Comptroller
v. Wynne (2015) confirmed that this structure satisfies the dormant Commerce Clause, as
long as the tax credit mechanisms make the statute internally consistent.34
The tax credit provisions of the BTA are broad and ensure that the tax would be
internally consistent. Section 50307(a) provides a general credit for taxes paid to other
states, with credits specifically apportioned based on part-year residencies, and Section
50307(b) directs an additional credit wherever the Constitution requires one. These credit
provisions eliminate the multiple-taxation exposure that the internal consistency test
targets.
Opponents of the BTA have come to a diZerent conclusion, in one case based on a
hypothetical where a person is a resident of two states for a single day. But that analysis
ignores that application of the internal-consistency test requires an assumption that all

28 Id. at 361–62.
29 Id. at 362.
30 Comptroller v. Wynne, 575 U.S. 542, 568 (2015).
31 BTA §§ 50308(a), 50301(a), 50303(c)(5).
32 See supra note 24.
33 BTA §§ 50306, 50307.
34 Wynne, 575 U.S. 542 (2015).
6
states have the exact same laws. That exercise would mean incorporating the BTA’s tax base,
apportionment percentages, and the California residency requirements that it uses. The
latter is particularly important because the California residency requirement is satisfied only
if an individual is in the state for other than a temporary or transitory purpose or if they are
domiciled in the state but outside the state for a temporary or transitory purpose.35 The
state’s regulations clarify that only one state, “the state in which a person has the closest
connection,” is the state of residence under that law.36 Therefore, if every state used the exact
same residency standard, there would be no situation where a person had two states of
residency for purposes of the tax. And there would concomitantly be no violation of the
internal consistency requirement. Here too, then, any plausible facial constitutional
infirmity is addressed by the tax credit provisions and the residency standard used.
The BTA also contains provisions that would remedy any potentially unconstitutional
apportionments of the tax. Specifically, section 50306(b) of the BTA contains an alternative
apportionment method that applies if the prescribed method does not “fairly represent” the
portion of the wealth that is taxable by California.37 The BTA also contains both a standard
for establishing that an alternative formula may be used and a provision that permits the use
of an alternative when a taxpayer shows that the standard method would violate federal law,
the U.S. Constitution, or the California Constitution.38 These provisions give taxpayers an as-
applied remedy for any unfair apportionment, which defeats a facial challenge to the
prescribed method.
Opponents also take exception to the provision of a “minimum” apportionment
percentage of twenty-five percent under the BTA’s alternative apportionment section. But
that minimum is not required in all cases. The BTA explicitly provides that the twenty-five
percent minimum can be waived if a lower percentage is required to avoid violating federal
law or the U.S. or California constitutions.39 On its face, then, the BTA provides a remedy for
any application that would violate federal law, and a facial challenge on this ground therefore
fails. As-applied challenges will turn on individual facts, but the statute supplies the
mechanism to resolve them.
Right to Interstate Travel
Opponents’ inventive right to travel argument is not supported by any relevant judicial
authority. The Supreme Court identifies three components to the constitutionally protected
35 Cal. Rev. & Tax’n Code §17014.
36 Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 18, § 17014.
37 BTA § 50306(b).
38 BTA § 50206(b)(3), (4).
39 BTA § 50306(b)(6).
7
right to travel: (1) the right to enter and leave another state, (2) the right when visiting another
state to enjoy the “privileges or immunities” that state grants its own citizens, and (3) the right
to become a citizen of a new state and have all the same rights as the existing citizens of that
state.40 The BTA does not interfere with any of these components of the right to travel.
The BTA does not prohibit, penalize, punish, or tax the right to enter and leave
California. It is not an “exit tax” on every person departing or passing through the state, as it
is not triggered by a taxpayer’s exit or departure like the tax invalidated in Crandall v.
Nevada.41 Instead, the tax obligation is triggered based on enjoying the benefits and
protections of California law as of the January 1, 2026 tax obligation date in accumulating
and sustaining wealth. It is irrelevant to the tax obligation whether the taxpayer billionaire
thereafter leaves the state. No precedent, constitutional text, or constitutional history
supports the opponents’ position that billionaires’ inability to wholly avoid the tax by
departing from California somehow restricts their ability to travel or move to another state.
The BTA also has no connection to the second and third components of the right to
travel. California is not denying anyone who visits the state the “privileges or immunities” it
grants its own citizens—instead, it is taxing certain of its citizens to pay their fair share of the
state’s financial needs. California also is not denying rights to newly arrived citizens through
the BTA. The BTA does not implicate the constitutional right to travel.
* * *
The primary federal constitutional arguments raised by opponents thus do not
facially invalidate the BTA. We also concur with the attached litigation risk assessment from
Gupta Wessler LLP that other potential federal constitutional challenges to the BTA are not
well taken. We believe that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial
challenges in a validation action or other similar proceeding.

Constitutional Flaws of California’s Proposed Wealth Tax
August 12, 2026 September 30, 2026 28 min read By: Jared Walczak (https://taxfoundation.org/about-us/staff/jared-walczak/) Download PDF (https://taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FF885_CA_Wealth_1.pdf)
Table of Contents
Key Findings
The California (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/) Billionaire Tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax/) A tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Act (Proposition 40), which imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ net worth, is vulnerable to numerous constitutional challenges, any of which could invalidate the tax in whole or in part.
Drafters’ characterization of the levy as an excise tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/excise-tax/) An excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. rather than a tax on property is irrelevant; if amendments superseding the state constitution’s limits on intangible property taxation fail, then the new tax fails as well.
The retroactive residency date is fatally flawed under Supreme Court precedent barring retroactive imposition of a “wholly new tax.”
The tax’s 100 percent apportionment (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/apportionment/) Apportionment is the determination of the percentage of a business’s profits subject to a given jurisdiction’s corporate income tax or other business tax. US states apportion business profits based on some combination of the percentage of company property, payroll, and sales located within their borders. system violates nexus, fair apportionment, and internal consistency requirements.
The measure’s sweeping anti-avoidance rules include assets the taxpayer does not own, raising due process issues and, in certain cases, guaranteeing double taxation (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/double-taxation/) Double taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. .
By seeking to lock taxpayers into full liability whether they stay or leave, the tax burdens the right to travel, which could force the state to defend these provisions under strict scrutiny.
The tax base (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax-base/) The tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. impermissibly includes US Treasuries and other federal obligations.
Uncapped penalties on appraisers who value hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns because they are grossly disproportionate to any good-faith errors.
Drafters have asked courts to reform the statute to cure any defects, but the measure’s constitutional flaws far exceed what can be accomplished through judicial reformation and point toward striking the tax down in its entirety.
Introduction
If California adopts a wealth tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/wealth-tax/) A wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary. , the only undisputed winners will be the lawyers. The California Billionaire Tax Act (CBTA), appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot as Proposition 40, is vulnerable to a range of legal challenges on numerous grounds and on multiple levels: as-applied challenges to the tax imposed on specific individuals; challenges to the validity of specific provisions as written, like the snapshot residency and valuation dates; and challenges to the constitutionality of the tax as a whole.
A prior paper examined how litigation over the CBTA’s residency and valuation provisions could require judicial reformation, eliminating some or all wealth tax liability for billionaires who leave the state in 2026—if the tax could survive such a challenge at all. [1] This paper explores the more fundamental question of whether the proposed wealth tax passes constitutional muster.
The measure’s drafters fully anticipated that their proposal would draw intense legal scrutiny and recognized that it would raise serious constitutional questions. They embedded a set of preemptive legal defenses into the tax’s design, attempting to insulate it from these challenges. But not all potential constitutional infirmities can be overcome by legal cunning, and the measure’s defensive provisions are an acknowledgment of a wealth tax’s fundamental legal vulnerabilities.
If courts invalidate the tax, California will have the worst of all worlds: a threat that drives away some of the state’s wealthiest taxpayers and spooks the next wave of startup founders, costly litigation that could drag on for years, and not a single dollar in new revenue. This is not a minor concern. The tax is legally dubious as well as economically damaging. This paper examines the legal deficiencies that could, and should, lead to the tax being struck down.
The Excise Tax Characterization Fails
The measure defines the wealth tax as an excise tax on the “activity” of “sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth.” [2] But courts, in California and at the federal level, have long held that the character of a tax is determined by its substance, not its form or label. [3] Merely calling a tax an excise tax does not make it one, and even if it is possible to define a tax as an excise in some fashion, it does not lose its ordinary characteristics.
A wealth tax is, fundamentally, a tax on property, and styling it as a tax on an “activity” does not change that fact, any more than ordinary real property taxes could be deemed to no longer be property taxes (and thus, perhaps, not subject to Proposition 13 assessment limits or rate caps) but rather an excise tax on the activity of sustaining ownership of real property. If excise tax framing can override the substance of a tax, that has implications for every taxpayer in California, because it could be used to avoid laws limiting any specific tax.
Fortunately, California and federal courts have historically disregarded labels when they conflict with the clear substance or nature of the tax in question, and it is a maxim of jurisprudence in California that “[t]he law respects form less than substance.” [4] The CBTA is a tax on both tangible and (especially) intangible property, with liability triggered by ownership on a fixed date, measured against net worth, and imposed without there being any transaction, transfer, or realization event. “Sustaining” accumulations of wealth is indistinguishable from ownership. The proposed wealth tax is a property tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/property-tax/) A property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. .
This matters because the state constitution imposes a 0.4 percent cap on the taxation of intangibles, and also requires taxes on property to be uniform, both of which undeniably conflict with the proposed wealth tax. [5] The measure’s drafters understood this, despite their efforts to frame the tax as an excise tax. They explicitly acknowledge the issue in one of their white papers on the proposal, [6] and their solution is to embed a constitutional amendment within the measure that authorizes this particular one-time tax notwithstanding any other provision of the constitution with which it might conflict.
Ballot measures are permitted to amend the constitution but not “revise” it—a distinction about how fundamental and sweeping the changes are. Some have suggested that the constitutional elements are broad enough to constitute an impermissible revision, and if courts came to that conclusion, then the state constitution’s limits on property taxation would apply to the tax, and its “excise tax” characterization is highly unlikely to save it. Similarly, courts may conclude that these constitutional amendments exceed what is permitted under the single subject rule for ballot initiatives, with the same result.
Meanwhile, the attempt to characterize the tax as an excise tax could backfire against proponents in federal constitutional litigation, because the whole framing of the tax is about taxing a status rather than a transaction or property ownership, which buttresses the case that this is a “wholly new tax”—a problem for its retroactivity, discussed below—and which complicates the tax’s already vexing apportionment problems.
The Retroactive Provisions Are Fatally Flawed
The CBTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who resided in California as of January 1, 2026, based on wealth measured on December 31, 2026. Since the measure is on the ballot in November, its residency snapshot predates the potential adoption of the tax by more than 10 months.
As noted in prior analyses, retroactivity is not necessarily a legal impediment by itself. Many taxes are modified retroactively in ways that have survived legal scrutiny. However, retroactivity has limits, some better defined than others. The period of retroactivity is a relevant consideration, but a period of less than a year is not unusual. Similarly, due process violations arise if “retroactive application is so harsh and oppressive as to transgress the constitutional limitation,” [7] which the courts would have to determine. Most pertinent for the wealth tax, however, is that the Supreme Court has distinguished between “modest” revisions of existing taxes and the adoption of a “wholly new tax,” [8] twice acting to strike down retroactive applications of a new tax—even when it only applied to periods when a taxpayer had good reason to believe that such a tax was forthcoming (“constructive notice”). [9]
The ordinary remedy for retroactivity is to exclusively apply the tax prospectively. Because the CBTA is designed as a one-time tax, however, this option is not readily available. The tax only contains one residency date, and it is retroactive. Invalidating any application prior to the November enactment date would therefore leave little, if any, of the tax intact.
Drafters knew the dates they chose invited such a challenge, and sought to build in a safety valve, asking courts to engage in “judicial reformation” to set later dates if these dates are deemed unconstitutional. The express request may help the case, but California’s courts have been reluctant to reform tax laws because they cannot reasonably anticipate whether lawmakers (or, in this case, voters) would have supported the measure had it been presented to them in revised form.
As the California appeals court noted in one such case, “In the context of cases involving tax statutes that violate the Commerce Clause, the courts have consistently declined to exercise the power of judicial reformation to cure the constitutional violation.” Rewriting a statute “would involve us in precisely the type of judicial policymaking and encroachment on the legislative function in violation of the separation of powers doctrine.” [10]

Constitutional Flaws of California’s Proposed Wealth Tax
August 12, 2026 September 30, 2026 28 min read By: Jared Walczak (https://taxfoundation.org/about-us/staff/jared-walczak/) Download PDF (https://taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FF885_CA_Wealth_1.pdf)
Table of Contents
Key Findings
The California (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/) Billionaire Tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax/) A tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Act (Proposition 40), which imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ net worth, is vulnerable to numerous constitutional challenges, any of which could invalidate the tax in whole or in part.
Drafters’ characterization of the levy as an excise tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/excise-tax/) An excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. rather than a tax on property is irrelevant; if amendments superseding the state constitution’s limits on intangible property taxation fail, then the new tax fails as well.
The retroactive residency date is fatally flawed under Supreme Court precedent barring retroactive imposition of a “wholly new tax.”
The tax’s 100 percent apportionment (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/apportionment/) Apportionment is the determination of the percentage of a business’s profits subject to a given jurisdiction’s corporate income tax or other business tax. US states apportion business profits based on some combination of the percentage of company property, payroll, and sales located within their borders. system violates nexus, fair apportionment, and internal consistency requirements.
The measure’s sweeping anti-avoidance rules include assets the taxpayer does not own, raising due process issues and, in certain cases, guaranteeing double taxation (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/double-taxation/) Double taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. .
By seeking to lock taxpayers into full liability whether they stay or leave, the tax burdens the right to travel, which could force the state to defend these provisions under strict scrutiny.
The tax base (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/tax-base/) The tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. impermissibly includes US Treasuries and other federal obligations.
Uncapped penalties on appraisers who value hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns because they are grossly disproportionate to any good-faith errors.
Drafters have asked courts to reform the statute to cure any defects, but the measure’s constitutional flaws far exceed what can be accomplished through judicial reformation and point toward striking the tax down in its entirety.
Introduction
If California adopts a wealth tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/wealth-tax/) A wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary. , the only undisputed winners will be the lawyers. The California Billionaire Tax Act (CBTA), appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot as Proposition 40, is vulnerable to a range of legal challenges on numerous grounds and on multiple levels: as-applied challenges to the tax imposed on specific individuals; challenges to the validity of specific provisions as written, like the snapshot residency and valuation dates; and challenges to the constitutionality of the tax as a whole.
A prior paper examined how litigation over the CBTA’s residency and valuation provisions could require judicial reformation, eliminating some or all wealth tax liability for billionaires who leave the state in 2026—if the tax could survive such a challenge at all. [1] This paper explores the more fundamental question of whether the proposed wealth tax passes constitutional muster.
The measure’s drafters fully anticipated that their proposal would draw intense legal scrutiny and recognized that it would raise serious constitutional questions. They embedded a set of preemptive legal defenses into the tax’s design, attempting to insulate it from these challenges. But not all potential constitutional infirmities can be overcome by legal cunning, and the measure’s defensive provisions are an acknowledgment of a wealth tax’s fundamental legal vulnerabilities.
If courts invalidate the tax, California will have the worst of all worlds: a threat that drives away some of the state’s wealthiest taxpayers and spooks the next wave of startup founders, costly litigation that could drag on for years, and not a single dollar in new revenue. This is not a minor concern. The tax is legally dubious as well as economically damaging. This paper examines the legal deficiencies that could, and should, lead to the tax being struck down.
The Excise Tax Characterization Fails
The measure defines the wealth tax as an excise tax on the “activity” of “sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth.” [2] But courts, in California and at the federal level, have long held that the character of a tax is determined by its substance, not its form or label. [3] Merely calling a tax an excise tax does not make it one, and even if it is possible to define a tax as an excise in some fashion, it does not lose its ordinary characteristics.
A wealth tax is, fundamentally, a tax on property, and styling it as a tax on an “activity” does not change that fact, any more than ordinary real property taxes could be deemed to no longer be property taxes (and thus, perhaps, not subject to Proposition 13 assessment limits or rate caps) but rather an excise tax on the activity of sustaining ownership of real property. If excise tax framing can override the substance of a tax, that has implications for every taxpayer in California, because it could be used to avoid laws limiting any specific tax.
Fortunately, California and federal courts have historically disregarded labels when they conflict with the clear substance or nature of the tax in question, and it is a maxim of jurisprudence in California that “[t]he law respects form less than substance.” [4] The CBTA is a tax on both tangible and (especially) intangible property, with liability triggered by ownership on a fixed date, measured against net worth, and imposed without there being any transaction, transfer, or realization event. “Sustaining” accumulations of wealth is indistinguishable from ownership. The proposed wealth tax is a property tax (https://taxfoundation.org/taxedu/glossary/property-tax/) A property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. .
This matters because the state constitution imposes a 0.4 percent cap on the taxation of intangibles, and also requires taxes on property to be uniform, both of which undeniably conflict with the proposed wealth tax. [5] The measure’s drafters understood this, despite their efforts to frame the tax as an excise tax. They explicitly acknowledge the issue in one of their white papers on the proposal, [6] and their solution is to embed a constitutional amendment within the measure that authorizes this particular one-time tax notwithstanding any other provision of the constitution with which it might conflict.
Ballot measures are permitted to amend the constitution but not “revise” it—a distinction about how fundamental and sweeping the changes are. Some have suggested that the constitutional elements are broad enough to constitute an impermissible revision, and if courts came to that conclusion, then the state constitution’s limits on property taxation would apply to the tax, and its “excise tax” characterization is highly unlikely to save it. Similarly, courts may conclude that these constitutional amendments exceed what is permitted under the single subject rule for ballot initiatives, with the same result.
Meanwhile, the attempt to characterize the tax as an excise tax could backfire against proponents in federal constitutional litigation, because the whole framing of the tax is about taxing a status rather than a transaction or property ownership, which buttresses the case that this is a “wholly new tax”—a problem for its retroactivity, discussed below—and which complicates the tax’s already vexing apportionment problems.
The Retroactive Provisions Are Fatally Flawed
The CBTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who resided in California as of January 1, 2026, based on wealth measured on December 31, 2026. Since the measure is on the ballot in November, its residency snapshot predates the potential adoption of the tax by more than 10 months.
As noted in prior analyses, retroactivity is not necessarily a legal impediment by itself. Many taxes are modified retroactively in ways that have survived legal scrutiny. However, retroactivity has limits, some better defined than others. The period of retroactivity is a relevant consideration, but a period of less than a year is not unusual. Similarly, due process violations arise if “retroactive application is so harsh and oppressive as to transgress the constitutional limitation,” [7] which the courts would have to determine. Most pertinent for the wealth tax, however, is that the Supreme Court has distinguished between “modest” revisions of existing taxes and the adoption of a “wholly new tax,” [8] twice acting to strike down retroactive applications of a new tax—even when it only applied to periods when a taxpayer had good reason to believe that such a tax was forthcoming (“constructive notice”). [9]
The ordinary remedy for retroactivity is to exclusively apply the tax prospectively. Because the CBTA is designed as a one-time tax, however, this option is not readily available. The tax only contains one residency date, and it is retroactive. Invalidating any application prior to the November enactment date would therefore leave little, if any, of the tax intact.
Drafters knew the dates they chose invited such a challenge, and sought to build in a safety valve, asking courts to engage in “judicial reformation” to set later dates if these dates are deemed unconstitutional. The express request may help the case, but California’s courts have been reluctant to reform tax laws because they cannot reasonably anticipate whether lawmakers (or, in this case, voters) would have supported the measure had it been presented to them in revised form.
As the California appeals court noted in one such case, “In the context of cases involving tax statutes that violate the Commerce Clause, the courts have consistently declined to exercise the power of judicial reformation to cure the constitutional violation.” Rewriting a statute “would involve us in precisely the type of judicial policymaking and encroachment on the legislative function in violation of the separation of powers doctrine.” [10]

The Federal Facial Constitutionality of California’s Proposed Billionaire
Tax Act
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act (BTA) authorizes a facial constitutional challenge to its
provisions by any interested person within sixty days of voter approval through a validation
action that does not impose a tax-prepayment requirement.1 To prevail in this facial
constitutional challenge, the interested person must establish that the BTA always operates
unconstitutionally and that judicial enforcement is constitutionally barred under any
potential set of circumstances.2
Some opponents of the Act urge that the Act should be rejected by California voters
due to federal constitutional infirmities with the Act that would render it facially invalid in
such an action. We believe, similar to the attached litigation risk assessment by Gupta
Wessler LLP, that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial challenges.
None of the opponents’ federal constitutional claims support that the BTA is facially
unconstitutional.
Retroactivity under the Due Process Clause
The BTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires residing in
California as of January 1, 2026, based on their wealth valued as of December 31, 2026. The
BTA thus locks in tax liability before voter approval of the tax.
The Supreme Court has explained that such retroactive application of a tax statute is
constitutional when “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational
means.”3 This standard is exceptionally deferential; the judiciary does not adjudge the
wisdom and fairness of taxation because such economic policy determinations “remain
with the exclusive province of the legislative and executive branches.”4 All retroactive
economic laws, including tax legislation, trigger this same deferential judicial scrutiny.5
Retroactive tax laws are thus upheld under the Due Process Clause unless the retroactive
application bears no rational relationship to a permissible legislative purpose.
The BTA’s look-back mechanism for triggering its tax obligation readily survives this
minimal due-process threshold. The state’s legitimate purpose is to ensure that individuals

same residency standard, there would be no situation where a person had two states of
residency for purposes of the tax. And there would concomitantly be no violation of the
internal consistency requirement. Here too, then, any plausible facial constitutional
infirmity is addressed by the tax credit provisions and the residency standard used.
The BTA also contains provisions that would remedy any potentially unconstitutional
apportionments of the tax. Specifically, section 50306(b) of the BTA contains an alternative
apportionment method that applies if the prescribed method does not “fairly represent” the
portion of the wealth that is taxable by California.37 The BTA also contains both a standard
for establishing that an alternative formula may be used and a provision that permits the use
of an alternative when a taxpayer shows that the standard method would violate federal law,
the U.S. Constitution, or the California Constitution.38 These provisions give taxpayers an as-
applied remedy for any unfair apportionment, which defeats a facial challenge to the
prescribed method.
Opponents also take exception to the provision of a “minimum” apportionment
percentage of twenty-five percent under the BTA’s alternative apportionment section. But
that minimum is not required in all cases. The BTA explicitly provides that the twenty-five
percent minimum can be waived if a lower percentage is required to avoid violating federal
law or the U.S. or California constitutions.39 On its face, then, the BTA provides a remedy for
any application that would violate federal law, and a facial challenge on this ground therefore
fails. As-applied challenges will turn on individual facts, but the statute supplies the
mechanism to resolve them.
Right to Interstate Travel
Opponents’ inventive right to travel argument is not supported by any relevant judicial
authority. The Supreme Court identifies three components to the constitutionally protected
35 Cal. Rev. & Tax’n Code §17014.
36 Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 18, § 17014.
37 BTA § 50306(b).
38 BTA § 50206(b)(3), (4).
39 BTA § 50306(b)(6).
7
right to travel: (1) the right to enter and leave another state, (2) the right when visiting another
state to enjoy the “privileges or immunities” that state grants its own citizens, and (3) the right
to become a citizen of a new state and have all the same rights as the existing citizens of that
state.40 The BTA does not interfere with any of these components of the right to travel.
The BTA does not prohibit, penalize, punish, or tax the right to enter and leave
California. It is not an “exit tax” on every person departing or passing through the state, as it
is not triggered by a taxpayer’s exit or departure like the tax invalidated in Crandall v.
Nevada.41 Instead, the tax obligation is triggered based on enjoying the benefits and
protections of California law as of the January 1, 2026 tax obligation date in accumulating
and sustaining wealth. It is irrelevant to the tax obligation whether the taxpayer billionaire
thereafter leaves the state. No precedent, constitutional text, or constitutional history
supports the opponents’ position that billionaires’ inability to wholly avoid the tax by
departing from California somehow restricts their ability to travel or move to another state.
The BTA also has no connection to the second and third components of the right to
travel. California is not denying anyone who visits the state the “privileges or immunities” it
grants its own citizens—instead, it is taxing certain of its citizens to pay their fair share of the
state’s financial needs. California also is not denying rights to newly arrived citizens through
the BTA. The BTA does not implicate the constitutional right to travel.
* * *
The primary federal constitutional arguments raised by opponents thus do not
facially invalidate the BTA. We also concur with the attached litigation risk assessment from
Gupta Wessler LLP that other potential federal constitutional challenges to the BTA are not
well taken. We believe that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial
challenges in a validation action or other similar proceeding.
Charles W. Rhodes Adam B. Thimmesch
Edward H. Hunvald Professor of Law Marga

The Federal Facial Constitutionality of California’s Proposed Billionaire
Tax Act
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act (BTA) authorizes a facial constitutional challenge to its
provisions by any interested person within sixty days of voter approval through a validation
action that does not impose a tax-prepayment requirement.1 To prevail in this facial
constitutional challenge, the interested person must establish that the BTA always operates
unconstitutionally and that judicial enforcement is constitutionally barred under any
potential set of circumstances.2
Some opponents of the Act urge that the Act should be rejected by California voters
due to federal constitutional infirmities with the Act that would render it facially invalid in
such an action. We believe, similar to the attached litigation risk assessment by Gupta
Wessler LLP, that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial challenges.
None of the opponents’ federal constitutional claims support that the BTA is facially
unconstitutional.
Retroactivity under the Due Process Clause
The BTA imposes a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires residing in
California as of January 1, 2026, based on their wealth valued as of December 31, 2026. The
BTA thus locks in tax liability before voter approval of the tax.
The Supreme Court has explained that such retroactive application of a tax statute is
constitutional when “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational
means.”3 This standard is exceptionally deferential; the judiciary does not adjudge the
wisdom and fairness of taxation because such economic policy determinations “remain
with the exclusive province of the legislative and executive branches.”4 All retroactive
economic laws, including tax legislation, trigger this same deferential judicial scrutiny.5
Retroactive tax laws are thus upheld under the Due Process Clause unless the retroactive
application bears no rational relationship to a permissible legislative purpose.
The BTA’s look-back mechanism for triggering its tax obligation readily survives this
minimal due-process threshold. The state’s legitimate purpose is to ensure that individuals

2 Wash. State Grange v. Wash. State Rep. Party, 552 U.S. 442, 449 (2008); United States v. Salerno, 481 U.S. 739,
745 (1987).
3 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26, 30-31 (1994) (quoting Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. v. R. A. Gray & Co.,
467 U.S. 717, 729-30 (1984) & Usery v. Turner Elkhorn Mining Co., 428 U.S. 1, 16-17 (1976)).
4 Id. at 31 (quoting Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp., 467 U.S. at 729-30 & Usery, 428 U.S. at 16-17 (1976)).
5 Id. at 30-31; see CHARLES W. RHODES & RENEE KNAKE JEFFERSON, CONSTITUTIONAL LAW: FOUNDATIONS,
INTERPRETATIONS, AND COMMENTARIES 528 (2025).
2
who accumulated and sustained immense wealth under the protection, infrastructure, and
economic benefits of California contribute their equitable share to critical public needs,
specifically healthcare, education, and nutrition. Raising revenue to fund state programs
and adjusting the tax burden are quintessential legitimate government purposes.6 California
has a strong interest in preventing the artificial erosion of its tax base for these purposes
through locking in the tax obligation as of January 1.
The retroactive period in the BTA is a rational means to accomplish this legitimate
purpose. It spans less than a single year to ensure that those benefiting from California’s
laws in accumulating and sustaining their wealth do not maneuver to avoid paying their fair
share. Because billionaires possess highly mobile assets, a wealth tax eZective only after
BTA’s passage would invite capital flight and portfolio restructuring. The look-back
mechanism is therefore an appropriate means to ensure that the tax base is not subverted
by short-term gamesmanship. The Supreme Court routinely upholds retroactive tax
applications of similar durations to avoid such gamesmanship.7
Opponents’ reliance on Nichols v. Coolidge (1927), Blodgett v. Holden (1927), and
Untermyer v. Anderson (1928) is misplaced. As the Supreme Court explained in United
States v. Carlton (1994), those cases were products of the Lochner era's rigid and long-
discarded judicial second-guessing of economic tax legislation through heighted judicial
scrutiny.8 Modern decisions merely require a rational basis for the retroactive application.9
While California did not previously tax the accumulation and maintenance of wealth,
aZected taxpayers possessed constructive notice of the potential for impending liability as
of the tax obligation date of January 1, 2026. Although opponents claim that the BTA is a
“wholly new tax” that cannot be retroactive under the holdings of two century-old Lochner-
era precedents, those cases have never been relied on again by the United States Supreme
Court to invalidate any tax as retroactive. The Court’s modern cases, such as United States
v. Darusmont, explain that, to the extent these century-old cases have any remaining vitality,
they would only apply when the taxpayer has “no reason to suppose that any transactions of

burden is a permissible legislative goal).
7 See United States v. Darusmont, 449 U.S. 292, 296–97 (1981) (customary congressional practice to make tax
statutes retroactive to the beginning of the calendar year or the date of introduction); Carlton, 512 U.S. at 32–
33 (upholding a 14-month retroactive period).
8 Carlton, 512 U.S. at 34 (“Those cases were decided during an era characterized by exacting review of
economic legislation under an approach that ‘has long since been discarded’” (quoting Ferguson v. Skrupa,
372 U.S. 726, 730 (1963)); see RHODES & JEFFERSON, supra n.5, at 521-28 (detailing the demise of economic
substantive due process).
9 E.g., Carlton, 512 U.S. at 30-34; Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp., 467 U.S. at 729; Quarty v. United States, 170
F.3d 961, 965 (9th Cir. 1999).
3
the sort will be taxed at all.”10 A statewide initiative requires public filing, title and summary
preparation, and months of highly publicized signature gathering before it ever reaches the
ballot, and the California legislature for several years before that considered wealth tax
proposals.11 Ballot proponents initially filed the BTA with the California Attorney General on
October 22, 2025, and amended the filing on November 26, 2025. A taxpayer is not unfairly
surprised when such a tax measure was a matter of active public debate during the period
of retroactivity.12
Finally, even assuming the United States Supreme Court overruled Carlton and
reinvigorated its 1920s decisions on retroactive tax liability, that would not render the BTA
facially invalid. A statute is facially invalid only if it is unconstitutional in all applications.13
Because federal constitutional facial challenges are “disfavored” by the Supreme Court,14 a
challenged law that is constitutional in at least some applications must be upheld.15 Any
judicial holding that the BTA operated impermissibly retroactively under those century-old
decisions when applying to some California billionaires who left the state before its passage
would not establish that the BTA was invalid in all its applications. This is especially true
because the BTA details that the Act’s provisions are severable and that the tax obligation
date is subject to judicial reformation to cure any constitutional infirmity.16

Some opponents have also claimed that the BTA would violate the fair apportionment
requirements of the Due Process and dormant Commerce Clauses of the U.S. Constitution.
Like the claims addressed in the prior part, those claims are not supported by established
Supreme Court precedent.

11 E.g., Assemb. B. 2088, 2019–2020 Leg., Reg. Sess. (Cal. 2020) (as amended Aug. 13, 2020); Assemb. B. 310,

Taxpayers who bring constitutional challenges to state apportionment methods face
a heavy burden.17 This is particularly true for facial challenges, as evidenced by the fact that
the Supreme Court has never held an apportionment formula unconstitutional on its face.18
The standards under the Due Process and dormant Commerce Clauses overlap. The
Due Process Clause requires only that the values being taxed are “rationally related to values
connected with the taxing state.”19 A taxpayer bringing a facial challenge to a statute under
that standard must show that the apportionment of the tax was “inherently arbitrary.”20 In
this context, the Court has said that state apportionment methods are “presumptively
valid.”21 The taxes that the Court has upheld under this standard are instructive. For example,
for corporate income tax purposes, the Court has repeatedly upheld the use of single-factor
methods while acknowledging that those methods do not produce results that represent
actual in-state profits.22 The use of a single factor, like sales, is not an inherently arbitrary
method, despite being an imprecise way to apportion income.
For personal income taxes, the Supreme Court has held that residence, standing
alone, is a constitutionally suZicient basis for taxing individuals on their income wherever
earned.23 The same principle applies to the taxation of intangible property. A state may tax a
resident’s intangible property wherever that property is located.24 As stated by the Court,
“[f]rom the beginning of our constitutional system control over the person at the place of his
domicile and his duty there, common to all citizens, to contribute to the support of
government have been deemed to aZord an adequate constitutional basis for imposing on
him a tax on the use and enjoyment of rights in intangibles measured by their value.”25 The
Court has recognized that this rule permits more than one state to tax the same intangibles
and has held that the resulting exposure to multiple taxation does not violate the Due
Process Clause.26
The risk of multiple taxation, or more precisely of higher burdens on interstate
commerce than on intrastate commerce, is more appropriately a dormant Commerce

burden of proof, and it is a very heavy burden indeed.”).
18 Id. at ¶ 8.13[2].
19 Moorman Mfg. Co. v. Bair, 437 U.S. 267, 273 (1978).
20 Id. at 274; Underwood Typewriter Co. v. Chamberlain, 254 U.S. 113, 121 (1920).
21 Id.
22 Moorman, 437 U.S. at 273.
23 New York ex rel. Cohn v. Graves, 300 U.S. 308 (1937).
24 See, e.g., Curry v. McCanless, 307 U.S. 357 (1939). Residence does not, however, support taxation of land or

25 Curry, 307 U.S. at 366.
26 Id. at 368–72.

Clause concern. Formally, the dormant Commerce Clause requires that state taxes be fairly
apportioned, which requires that a statute be both externally and internally consistent.27 The
external consistency test is functionally the same as the Due Process “rationally related”
test.28 The internal consistency test is diZerent. That test looks to whether the tax, if applied
by every jurisdiction, would result in higher tax burdens on interstate commerce as
compared to purely intrastate commerce.29 Internal consistency can be met in several ways,
including by apportioning taxes or by using unapportioned taxes along with tax credits for
taxes imposed by other states on the same base.30
The BTA meets these Due Process and dormant Commerce Clause standards. To
start, the BTA would apply only to California residents as of the tax obligation date and would
be imposed on “net worth,” which is defined to exclude tangible property located outside of
the state.31 Residence therefore supplies the constitutional basis the Due Process Clause
requires, and the exclusion of out-of-state tangible property keeps the tax within the rule
described above.32
The BTA would also be apportioned in a constitutional manner. The tax apportions
100% of the tax base to California, but it also provides taxpayers with credits against the
resulting tax for taxes paid to other states on the same base. 33 That structure is no diZerent
from the structure that states use for purposes of their personal income taxes. Comptroller
v. Wynne (2015) confirmed that this structure satisfies the dormant Commerce Clause, as
long as the tax credit mechanisms make the statute internally consistent.34
The tax credit provisions of the BTA are broad and ensure that the tax would be
internally consistent. Section 50307(a) provides a general credit for taxes paid to other
states, with credits specifically apportioned based on part-year residencies, and Section
50307(b) directs an additional credit wherever the Constitution requires one. These credit
provisions eliminate the multiple-taxation exposure that the internal consistency test
targets.

hypothetical where a person is a resident of two states for a single day. But that analysis
ignores that application of the internal-consistency test requires an assumption that all

28 Id. at 361–62.
29 Id. at 362.

32 See supra note 24.

latter is particularly important because the California residency requirement is satisfied only
if an individual is in the state for other than a temporary or transitory purpose or if they are
domiciled in the state but outside the state for a temporary or transitory purpose.35 The
state’s regulations clarify that only one state, “the state in which a person has the closest
connection,” is the state of residence under that law.36 Therefore, if every state used the exact
same residency standard, there would be no situation where a person had two states of
residency for purposes of the tax. And there would concomitantly be no violation of the
internal consistency requirement. Here too, then, any plausible facial constitutional
infirmity is addressed by the tax credit provisions and the residency standard used.
The BTA also contains provisions that would remedy any potentially unconstitutional
apportionments of the tax. Specifically, section 50306(b) of the BTA contains an alternative
apportionment method that applies if the prescribed method does not “fairly represent” the
portion of the wealth that is taxable by California.37 The BTA also contains both a standard
for establishing that an alternative formula may be used and a provision that permits the use
of an alternative when a taxpayer shows that the standard method would violate federal law,
the U.S. Constitution, or the California Constitution.38 These provisions give taxpayers an as-
applied remedy for any unfair apportionment, which defeats a facial challenge to the
prescribed method.
Opponents also take exception to the provision of a “minimum” apportionment
percentage of twenty-five percent under the BTA’s alternative apportionment section. But
that minimum is not required in all cases. The BTA explicitly provides that the twenty-five
percent minimum can be waived if a lower percentage is required to avoid violating federal
law or the U.S. or California constitutions.39 On its face, then, the BTA provides a remedy for
any application that would violate federal law, and a facial challenge on this ground therefore
fails. As-applied challenges will turn on individual facts, but the statute supplies the
mechanism to resolve them.

authority. The Supreme Court identifies three components to the constitutionally protected

state to enjoy the “privileges or immunities” that state grants its own citizens, and (3) the right
to become a citizen of a new state and have all the same rights as the existing citizens of that
state.40 The BTA does not interfere with any of these components of the right to travel.
The BTA does not prohibit, penalize, punish, or tax the right to enter and leave
California. It is not an “exit tax” on every person departing or passing through the state, as it
is not triggered by a taxpayer’s exit or departure like the tax invalidated in Crandall v.
Nevada.41 Instead, the tax obligation is triggered based on enjoying the benefits and
protections of California law as of the January 1, 2026 tax obligation date in accumulating
and sustaining wealth. It is irrelevant to the tax obligation whether the taxpayer billionaire
thereafter leaves the state. No precedent, constitutional text, or constitutional history
supports the opponents’ position that billionaires’ inability to wholly avoid the tax by
departing from California somehow restricts their ability to travel or move to another state.

travel. California is not denying anyone who visits the state the “privileges or immunities” it
grants its own citizens—instead, it is taxing certain of its citizens to pay their fair share of the
state’s financial needs. California also is not denying rights to newly arrived citizens through
the BTA. The BTA does not implicate the constitutional right to travel.

The primary federal constitutional arguments raised by opponents thus do not
facially invalidate the BTA. We also concur with the attached litigation risk assessment from
Gupta Wessler LLP that other potential federal constitutional challenges to the BTA are not
well taken. We believe that the Act would be upheld against federal constitutional facial
challenges in a validation action or other similar proceeding.

Constitutional Flaws of California’s Proposed Wealth Tax
August 12, 2026 September 30, 2026 28 min read By: Jared Walczak (https://taxfoundation.org/about-us/staff/jared-walczak/) Download PDF (https://taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FF885_CA_Wealth_1.pdf)
