Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.

This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.
See this Liberty Lens essay (https://libertylensecon.substack.com/p/california-wealth-tax-npv) for a summary of the paper's findings.

The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
Section-by-Section Summary
Introduction to this summary. This document has been prepared by the drafters of
Proposition 40, the California Billionaire Tax Act (“Prop 40”), to explain its details in
plain English to voters and other interested parties, such as legislators, regulators and
taxpayers. It is being submitted as public testimony and posted publicly.
This summary describes the ordinary meaning of Prop 40. California courts will use
ordinary principles of constitutional and statutory interpretation, including construing the
“plain and ordinary meaning,” to resolve any disputes about what Prop 40 does. Critics of
Prop 40 have posted claims about the measure that differ at points with this summary. In
our view these claims rest on implausible and often unreasonable efforts to twist the plain
language and intent of Prop 40. California courts have rejected the use of strained,
unreasonable arguments to conjure up ambiguity and thus these contrary accounts should
be rejected. In the event that courts do find some Prop 40 language ambiguous, we expect
they will rely in part on this summary and other interpretations offered by the drafters.
California courts attempt to honor voters’ intentions, and so have generally held drafters
to the claims about an initiative that they have made publicly to voters.1 In addition, a
ballot initiative that can be read and readily understood by voters cannot address every
conceivable complex legal question that might arise, and so the drafters expect that some
highly technical issues, such as the treatment of property held through single-member
LLCs, may be resolved through further guidance from California tax regulators.
Prop 40 Overview.2 The Act is a one-time wealth tax initiative for tax year 2026.
Revenues from the one-time tax are committed to address an urgent and pressing fiscal
emergency caused by the expected imminent loss of about $100 billion in federal funding
for health care, education, and nutrition programs. The tax portion of the Act (i) imposes
a 5% excise tax on California-resident billionaires on their worldwide net worth of as of
December 31, 2026, payable at once, or over 5 years with a deferral charge; (ii) defines a
California-resident billionaire as a billionaire who resided in California as of January 1,
2026; (iii) allows taxpayers who do not have cash available to pay the tax to defer
payment until later, with an interest charge; and (iv) further offers optional deferral
accounts for qualifying taxpayers.
Structure. The measure is implemented through (A) a constitutional amendment (new
Article XIII, Section 37) authorizing the tax and creating a dedicated Reserve Fund; (B) a

Government Code article establishing Reserve Fund subaccounts and
appropriation/reporting rules for that fund that will be primarily dedicated to health care,

Sec. 1. Title
Provides that Prop 40 may be cited as the “2026 Billionaire Tax Act.”
Sec. 2. Findings
The findings describe urgent and pressing (and in that sense, one-time) threats to
California’s health care, education, and nutrition assistance systems arising from an
expected $100 billion in federal funding cuts affecting Medi-Cal, California public
schools, and CalFresh/SNAP.
Sec. 3. Purpose and Intent
The purpose of Prop 40 is to raise revenue to fund health care, K-14 education, and food
assistance through levying a one-time, administrable, and fair tax on California
billionaires. The billionaire taxpayers are most able to pay the tax, and also generally pay
much less in taxes relative to their ability to pay compared to many other Californians.
Because there are urgent and pressing threats to California’s health care, education, and
nutrition assistance systems arising from an expected $100 billion in federal funding cuts,
and because a one-time tax can be set up and administered much more quickly to begin
raising revenues sooner, the one-time structure of the tax is best suited to the imminent
fiscal emergency.
Sec. 4. Constitutional Authorization and Dedicated Reserve Fund.
Section 4 adds Section 37 to the California Constitution, which grants constitutional
authorization for the wealth tax. As described in greater detail below, it also provides for
the creation of a Reserve Fund and permits facial challenges to the law to be adjudicated
through a validation action proceeding.
• Use of funds. California’s constitution contains numerous complicated fiscal
rules, including caps on state expenditures. Such rules and limits were not
designed to account for emergencies of the type created by recent massive federal
funding cuts. As a result of these cuts, California needs to significantly increase
its expenditures to maintain the same baseline of services. Accordingly, this
section assures that proceeds from Prop 40 will be expended to mitigate the
impact of the federal cuts. Proceeds from the tax are placed in a new Reserve
Fund that is permanently separate from the General Fund, with 90% committed to
health care; and 10% to K-14 education and food assistance, all for the benefit of
low and moderate-income families and individuals.
3
• Legal challenges. Generally, as a matter of California constitutional law,
challenges to taxation can only be made after a tax is paid. In order to provide for
more fiscal certainty for the Legislature, this section amends those rules to permit
certain legal challenges to be brought immediately and to have a speedier
resolution, through the California courts. The provision is based on validation
actions, described more in the discussion of Operative Tax Provisions at Section
50314.
Sec. 5. Reserve Fund Implementation in the Government Code.
Section 16355
Creates the operational rules for the Reserve Fund and its two subaccounts, the Health
Account and the Education and Food Assistance Account. The permitted uses of the tax
revenue in the subaccounts are defined broadly.
For the Health Account, which shall receive 90% of the tax revenue, permitted uses
include restoring or addressing reductions in federal funding or state appropriations;
protecting and enhancing Medi-Cal and other coverage programs; supporting safety net
providers; preventing or mitigating facility closures or service reductions; and other
investments supporting health care access, coverage, benefits, funding, services, and
provider payments.
As for the Education and Food Assistance Account, which shall receive 10% of the tax
revenue, permitted uses include education spending to restore or address reductions in
federal or state funding or to protect/enhance the K–14 public education system; and food
assistance spending to restore or address reductions in federal or state funding or to invest
in programs like CalFresh, and California’s Universal Meals Program.
This section also limits how much anticipated revenue the Legislature can spend in one
year (up to $25 billion/year) to provide for spending over a five-year period. It also
forbids the Legislature from using this new revenue to replace existing state funds.
At subdivision (e), the section provides funds for tax administration. The Franchise Tax
Board (“Board”) is charged with administering the tax. This section provides the Board
with a start-up loan of up to $50 million to implement Prop 40, as well as an ongoing
annual reimbursement from the Reserve Fund for actual and necessary administrative and
evaluation costs.
Subdivision (f) describes how the Department of Finance must report annually to the
Legislature regarding the Reserve Fund, including the Fund balance, the estimated
revenue to be generated for the Fund and proposed expenditures from the Fund. The
Department also shall verify that moneys from the Reserve Fund are not being used to
replace existing state funding. After the Director of Finance determines that all revenues
from the Act have been collected and spent, under subdivision (g) the Legislature has the
authority to abolish the Reserve Fund. Subdivision (h) provides definitions for this
section.
4
Sec. 6. Operative Tax Provisions
Part. 27. 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
Chapter 1. Imposition of Tax on Personal Wealth in Excess of $1 Billion in Net
Worth
Section 50300. Short title
Provides that Part 27 is known, and may be cited, as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Section 50301. Imposition of tax; rate and phase-in; payment; filing; audit
Subdivision (a): One-time excise tax; determination dates; married couples.
This subdivision imposes, for tax year 2026, an excise tax on the “activity of sustaining
excessive accumulations of wealth” by California residents with worldwide net worth of
$1 billion or more. Net worth includes all assets, whether tangible or financial, except for
certain exceptions described in more detail below. Recent data suggest as much as three-
quarters of current billionaire wealth is in the form of stock of publicly-traded companies.
In order to prevent the misuse of trusts to avoid the tax, this subdivision also imposes tax
on any trust to which a living California billionaire has transferred assets; these trusts are
described in more detail in Section 50308 below.
Whether a person is a California resident is determined as of the “tax obligation date”
(January 1, 2026), while the amount of net worth subject to tax is measured as of the
“valuation date” (December 31, 2026). The timing for determining whether a trust is an
applicable trust is discussed under Section 50308 below.
Subdivision (b): 5% tax; phase-in between $1.0B and $1.1B; ODA carve-out.
• Tax rate. This subdivision sets the tax rate at 5% of net worth for individuals with
net worth in excess of $1 billion and covered trusts. For fairness, the full rate
phases in linearly for taxpayers with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion
(with respect to individuals other than trusts).
• Deferral for illiquid taxpayers. Allows an individual who lacks current liquid
assets to pay the tax to opt to initiate an Optional Deferral Account (“ODA”)
under Section 50304 to defer paying tax until the time specified by Section 50304.
ODAs are discussed in greater detail in Section 50304.
Subdivision (c): Return filing and timing; installment option and deferral charge.
This subdivision provides that additional tax payable under Section 50301 (and under
Section 50304 [the ODA provision], if applicable) is reported with, and due at the same
time as, the taxpayer’s annual personal income tax return. A taxpayer may either pay the
tax in full with the 2026 return or elect to pay in five equal annual installments beginning
5
in the year the tax is due. Each subsequent annual installment is subject to an annual
nondeductible “deferral charge” equal to 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.
Subdivision (d): Filing requirement / certification.
This subdivision requires every California resident individual who files an income tax
return for 2026 to either (i) make a simple declaration as part of the individual’s annual
tax filings (like the checkbox declarations of a taxpayer’s filing status or dependent
status) that the individual’s net assets were less than or equal to $1 billion as of the
valuation date or (ii) submit a declaration of the additional tax owed under Part 27,
together with required Board forms and supporting valuation evidence (including
certified appraisals where required).
Subdivision (e): Franchise Tax Board examination obligation and powers.
This subdivision directs the Board to examine all returns submitted under Part 27 and to
determine the correct amount of tax owed by billionaires. The Board is not required to
audit taxpayers who check the box to indicate they are not billionaires and is granted no
new authority for audits generally. There are not expected to be many such returns and
the FTB will be given more resources (see proposed Government Code Section 16355(e)
above), and time to complete audits (see Section 50309(b)(3)). Subdivision (e)(2)
specifies that the Board has discretion over the length of any such audit.
Chapter 2. Computation of Net Worth
Section 50302. Debts and liabilities
• Calculation of net worth. Prop 40 imposes a tax on a taxpayer’s net worth and
thus the Act reduces, with certain limitations, the taxable wealth by the amount of
any liability that is personally owed by the taxpayer. Legally enforceable
charitable pledges entered into before October 15, 2025 also reduce net worth.
• Genuine debts and certain other liabilities reduce net worth. Debt can be used to
artificially reduce taxpayer net worth to an extent that does not reflect economic
reality, however. Thus, the amount of any nonrecourse or limited recourse debt
that reduces net worth may not exceed the value included in the taxpayer’s net
worth for the collateral securing that debt. For the same reasons, contingent
liabilities, liabilities owed to related parties or otherwise not at arms’ length, and
debts with an interest rate below market generally do not reduce net worth. Other
liabilities entered into for the purpose of reducing tax may also be disregarded
under the general anti-avoidance rules described in Section 50312, below.
Section 50303. Valuation rules; exclusions; asset-type rules
Subdivision (a): Fair market value standard.
Adopts, with certain technical modifications, the standard tax definition of fair market
value: the price a willing and informed buyer would pay a willing and informed seller.
6
Subdivision (b): Anti-abuse rules.
Disallows certain legal structures taxpayers commonly use to reduce the taxable value of
an asset. In particular, this section is intended to disallow two common techniques used
by very wealthy taxpayers to reduce the valuation of an estate that would otherwise be
subject to estate tax. The drafters specifically intend that prior opinions of the U.S. Tax
Court upholding these techniques, which commenters generally agree were wrongly
decided, should not govern interpretation of Prop 40.
Subdivision (c): Asset-type valuation rules, exclusions, and reporting requirements.
This subdivision provides default valuation methods, exclusions, and reporting
requirements for specific asset types.
1. Publicly traded assets — “market trading value on the valuation date” (Section
50303(c)(1))
For all publicly traded assets, fair market value is presumed to be the asset’s market
trading value on December 31, 2026. The drafters expect that assets that are not publicly
traded but readily convertible to a publicly traded asset will have a value of not less than
the value of the publicly traded asset.
Prop 40 uses market pricing on the valuation date of December 31, 2026 for publicly
traded assets because those assets have readily ascertainable values through active
markets, reducing the need for appraisal-based valuation and lowering administrative and
compliance costs. Also, a taxpayer has the option of selling a portion of such assets on
the valuation date to effectively lock in the market value on the valuation date. Although
Prop 40 does not specify the precise convention for determining “market trading value”
(for example, closing price, a volume-weighted average price, the mean of high and low
prices, or a bid/ask midpoint when no trades occur), the Board may specify such
conventions by regulation or other guidance, including rules for thin trading, multiple
exchanges, and days on which there is no trading. In that respect, federal estate and gift
tax valuation precedents for publicly traded securities (particularly Treasury Regulation
§§ 20.2031-2 and 25.2512-2) provide a reasonable reference point for these valuation
issues. The Board has general authority to promulgate such guidance under Section
50309(b), but is also specifically instructed to look to federal regulations in a related
context at Section 50305(b).
2. Sole proprietorships (Section 50303(c)(2))
Treats assets held through a sole proprietorship as directly owned and held by the
taxpayer.
3. Non-public business entity interests — “Presumed Percentage Method” and rebuttable
presumptions (Section 50303(c)(3))
Governs valuation of interests in business entities (including equity, debt, and other
contractual or noncontractual interests) that are not (i) interests in publicly traded

companies; or (ii) sole proprietorship assets. These default rules are designed to reduce
compliance and audit costs by allowing valuation based on standardized information
from financial statements. These simplified values are presumptions for administrative

The core dispute is between the proponents, who estimate about $100B with a 10% cut for avoidance, and Rauh et al., who put wealth tax revenue at $30-40B and find a negative net present value of $25-39B once lost income tax revenue is counted.

I'm weighing the LAO's figure of tens of billions against its under-$1B annual loss, and a rough present-value check suggests the measure could still come out modestly positive. I'm also noting that departures before January 1, 2026, like Page, Brin, and Thiel, have already happened and wouldn't be reversed by a no vote, though I'm wondering whether some might return if the measure fails.

Passage would bring one-time revenue in the tens of billions per the LAO, but it would also likely trigger major litigation over retroactive residency, due process, and the dormant commerce clause, and the tax could be partly or fully struck down. I'm also weighing whether the signal of a wealth tax would push more founders and billionaires out over time, which is the main economic argument against it.

I'm noting the practical costs of passage: future departures of billionaires and founders, and the possibility that the measure would discourage startups from locating in California. I'm also looking at a point about private companies, where the valuation method could tax founders with voting control on value they don't economically own, which would weigh heavily on startups.

I'm checking the rest of the Prop 40 consequences, starting with how private company valuation could hit founders who hold voting control but little economic stake. The rebuttal for that is an appraisal process, and I'm noting that if you're illiquid, a separate deferral option applies. If the measure fails, the state would have to find Medi-Cal funding elsewhere or make cuts, and billionaires who already left might or might not come back, while the rejection itself could signal a friendlier business climate. I'm weighing that against the value question, since the one-word answer the user wants depends on which outcomes matter more to them.

I'm checking which groups are on each side: economists across the spectrum look skeptical, Newsom and both gubernatorial candidates oppose it, and several health and teacher groups do too, which is notable since they would seem to gain from the revenue. Supporters include SEIU-UHW, Sanders, the nurses' association, and Ro Khanna.

I'm going to check the editorial endorsements from the major California papers and balanced analyses from groups like the Tax Policy Center, Brookings, and PPIC. I also want to find out whether the election has already happened, since the answer to how to vote depends on that.

Two economists studied California's billionaire tax. They reached wildly different conclusions
November 2, 2026 6:30 AM ET
Greg Rosalsky (https://www.npr.org/people/726239784/greg-rosalsky)

In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.
As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/20/nx-s1-5935597/california-billionaires-wealth-tax-sergey-brin) California since the tax was proposed.
Sponsor Message
On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) and podcast (https://www.npr.org/2019/07/24/744962126/episode-929-could-a-wealth-tax-work)). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires (https://gabriel-zucman.eu/we-need-to-tax-billionaires/). Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.
"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money .
On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.
Sponsor Message
" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."
It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html) in The New York Times .
A golden opportunity in the Golden State?
The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.
A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. That said, most of the wealth held by California billionaires is in publicly traded stocks, whose value is easy to determine.
Zucman, together with Jasper Boll and Emmanuel Saez, released an analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) of the California billionaire class and this proposed wealth tax.
Sponsor Message
"California billionaires' wealth has reached $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, as large as all the annual income reported on income tax returns of all Californians," they wrote. They found that California billionaire wealth had exploded by 144% between 2023 and 2025, thanks largely to the AI boom. "Over the longer run, the real wealth of California's billionaire class — the top 0.001% richest households — has been multiplied by 25 from 1982 to 2026, while average real family income in California has only doubled."
Zucman says a crucial problem with the existing tax system in California, America, and beyond is that the superrich have been seeing their wealth snowball bigger and bigger while paying relatively little in income taxes. Billionaires can structure their finances to generate little or no taxable income, making the income tax rate "totally irrelevant," he argues. Zucman believes a wealth tax will help address this, thereby helping to fight rising inequality, counteract the political power of "the oligarchs," and raise much-needed funds for everyone else.
Zucman, Boll, and Saez estimated that the state wealth tax proposed by Prop 40 could raise "about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax revenue." They arrive at that figure by taking 5% of their $2.3 trillion estimate of billionaire wealth, then reducing the projected revenue by 10% to account for avoidance, evasion, and the possibility that some billionaires ended their California residency before January 1, 2026.
Rauh argues that this 10% reduction to account for billionaires avoiding the tax is too optimistic.
Why past wealth taxes have been "abject failures"
As we've previously reported (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/newsletter/money), wealth taxes have been tried before around the world and they have had a dismal track record. Even Zucman, a wealth tax champion, writes in his new book that past wealth taxes "by and large, have been abject failures."
Zucman and his coterie of other (typically French) economists have spent a lot of time studying why past wealth taxes failed and have sought to design new ones that address those failures.
Sponsor Message
One crucial problem was that wealth taxes tended to have loopholes that allowed the rich to shelter their assets, making these taxes a leaky bucket. For example, before France scrapped its wealth tax back in 2018 (https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/11415-PGP.html/identifiant%3DACTU-2018-00087?utm_source=chatgpt.com), it exempted qualifying business assets, including shares in companies their owners ran. That, Zucman says, was a big loophole that drastically reduced the amount of revenue it raised.
Another crucial problem — which is at the center of the debate on this California wealth tax proposal — is that some superrich people move to avoid the tax. France became a cautionary tale, with critics often pointing to estimates that tens of thousands (https://www.mediapart.fr/en/journal/france/090815/rising-number-wealthy-french-fleeing-abroad?utm_source=chatgpt.com) of millionaires left while its wealth tax was in place. However, how much of that exodus was caused by the wealth tax remains disputed.
Zucman acknowledges that the flight of rich people has been an issue with past wealth taxes, but he also argues that this problem has been overblown. He, for example, pointed to a recent working paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35854?utm_source=chatgpt.com) about Norway, which has had a wealth tax since 1892 (https://www.reuters.com/business/norways-wealth-tax-trades-millionaires-equality-2025-11-24/). It found that recent increases to this existing wealth tax, alongside other tax increases on the rich, drove at most 100 rich people to leave. But, it found, those departures didn't do much to dent the resulting gains in wealth-tax revenue. That said, Norway is a nation, not a state, and moving to another country is a bigger deal than, say, moving from California to Nevada.
To avoid the failures of past wealth taxes, Prop 40's designers have tried to plug potential leaks. Unlike France's old wealth tax, it would tax business holdings, including shares in companies that billionaires run. And by making it a one-time, retroactive tax tied to where billionaires lived on January 1, 2026, they hope to prevent billionaires from escaping the bill by simply moving away.
Sponsor Message
However, whether these provisions will actually work is at the heart of the debate.
Are Prop 40 supporters just California Dreamin'?
Rauh recently released a competing analysis with a provocative conclusion: instead of raising $100 billion, as Zucman and the measure's supporters claim, this wealth tax could ultimately cost the state billions.
First, Rauh argues, at least seven famous billionaires had already left California before the January 1, 2026, residency cutoff, putting their fortunes beyond the tax's reach. Those billionaires are Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, and David Sacks.
Those departures alone, Rauh says, reduced the potential revenue from this wealth tax by "around $30 billion."
Zucman, however, disputes that those fortunes are beyond California's reach. He says the legal experts he trusts (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/podcast-episode/professor-brian-galle-how-to-tax-the-ultrarich-voices-carry/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) believe it's unlikely that any of these billionaires successfully ended their California tax residency before the cutoff. Ending your residency, he argues, takes more than a last-minute move across state lines. Prop 40 was designed with this in mind. It was announced in late October 2025 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-40-one?utm_source=chatgpt.com), giving billionaires only about two months to establish residency elsewhere before January 1, 2026. Talk about a New Year's Day hangover.
Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Sure, he's moved just across the border to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe — and meanwhile spent more than a hundred million dollars (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/g-s1-138201/california-billionaire-tax-google-sergey-brin) trying to defeat Prop 40. But, Zucman says, he still frequently commutes to work in Silicon Valley. A quick change of address, he argues, doesn't necessarily mean you've left California behind for tax purposes. Rauh counters that Brin, backed by what we can only assume are the best accountants and lawyers, has likely succeeded in establishing Nevada residency. He stands by his assumption that Brin and the others are beyond the tax's reach.
Like much of the debate over how much this tax will ultimately raise, this dispute has as much to do with the law as it does economics.
Sponsor Message
Which leads us to the second reason Rauh believes this proposed wealth tax will raise much less money than its supporters hope: the courts. Billionaires, armed with the best lawyers money can buy, will mount a slew of constitutional challenges to this tax. And given this wealth tax's novelty — and the Supreme Court's conservative majority — there's a real risk that at least part of Prop 40 could be struck down.
For example, Prop 40's controversial retroactive provision. It would tax some billionaires based on where they used to live. Rauh argues that could violate the Constitution's due process protections, although the Supreme Court has upheld other retroactive taxes (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/512/26/) in the past. The tax also reaches beyond California's borders, targeting wealth held around the world, which could create legal issues. Rauh also raises legal concerns about how the tax would value privately held companies. He says that venture capital deals can put a price on a company that overstates what it's actually worth. Taxing an owner's share of that inflated value, he argues, could create constitutional problems.
The architects of Prop 40 designed the law with legal challenges in mind, and it has all sorts of fallback provisions meant to keep the tax working if the courts strike down any part of it. But how much revenue would survive those legal battles? This is another big disagreement between Rauh and Zucman.
Rauh and Jaros estimate a big range of possible outcomes. But their central estimate, which has generated plenty of headlines, cuts the remaining projected revenue in half to account for legal uncertainty. That is a strong assumption — not a certainty about how the courts will rule — and Zucman disputes it.
After accounting for billionaire departures and the anticipated legal challenges, Rauh and Jaros estimate the wealth tax would bring in only "around $30 billion."
Sponsor Message
But that's not the end of their gloomy estimate. Because Rauh and Jaros expect even more billionaires to flee the state if Prop 40 passes, taking their existing income tax payments with them.

Rauh's answer: because they will rationally fear that this won't be the last wealth tax that California passes. The sense that California is becoming a hostile environment for the superrich could drive departures even if another wealth tax never materializes, he argues. After all, Zucman and many other supporters of Prop 40 see this one-time tax as only the beginning. Zucman advocates for an annual wealth tax in his book, and he told us, yeah, he doesn't really want this to be a one-time tax.
The way Rauh sees it, Prop 40 trades a stream of income-tax revenue in the future for a more immediate payout of wealth-tax revenue today. His calculation assumes those income tax losses continue indefinitely. All of which is how he and Jaros arrive at their shocking conclusion: "On net, the state loses $39 billion in expectation because of this tax," Rauh argues.
Zucman objects that their calculation factors in future income tax losses from billionaires fleeing feared wealth taxes — but none of the revenue those hypothetical wealth taxes would bring in.
"That's absurdly one-sided," Zucman says. "You can't just count the loss and not the gain."
Zucman also argues that the income tax losses from departing billionaires would be smaller than Rauh predicts. Using public financial disclosures, his team estimates that some of the richest billionaires — including Larry Page and Sergey Brin — pay relatively little in income taxes.
Rauh defends their calculation, arguing it follows standard procedures for scoring tax proposals. "It would be absurd to count revenue from not yet proposed taxes," he says. He also argues that the public financial disclosures Zucman and his team focus on give an incomplete picture of how much billionaires pay in income taxes.
Sponsor Message
The pull Of Silicon Valley
How much income tax revenue California could lose depends not just on what billionaires currently pay, but also on how many leave if Prop 40 passes. And the state has a powerful magnet that could keep them there: its thriving tech ecosystem.
For years, conservatives have been painting California as a progressive basket case, predicting that Democratic mismanagement would plunge its economy down the tubes and send rich people fleeing. Yet the state has become the epicenter of the AI boom. In 2025, Bay Area companies attracted three-quarters of all U.S. AI funding (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/BayArea-ReadyForRebound-SFBT-SR.pdf) — and more than half the worldwide total — according to the Bay Area Council Economic Institute.
Economists refer to this industrial clustering as "agglomeration." Companies, workers, and investors in the same industry benefit from being near one another. It's like a gigantic magnet for economic activity. Zucman suggests these agglomeration effects are so strong that billionaires will still want to live and work in California even if there is a wealth tax.
Zucman points to Mark Zuckerberg as an example. Rather than simply leaving California, Zuckerberg reportedly struck a deal (https://apnews.com/article/zuckerberg-california-billionaire-tax-meta-stock-shares-56be13ddd072b48578d14a8f9d7eb23f) with Meta's board that would let him pay the tax without sacrificing control of his company. Essentially, the deal would let him sell nonvoting shares to cover his potential wealth tax bill while holding on to enough voting shares to keep control of the company. In return, he agreed to stay in California for eight years, subject to conditions, including Meta remaining headquartered there.
Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, told Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-06/nvidia-ceo-says-he-s-perfectly-fine-with-billionaires-tax) in January that he was "perfectly fine" with paying the wealth tax envisioned by Prop 40. Under it, he would be on the hook for something like $8 billion. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Huang said. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."
Sponsor Message
Rauh, however, doubts that California's tech ecosystem has enough gravity to keep billionaires there if the tax passes. "Agglomeration effects are fragile," he argues. A wealth tax could saddle startup founders with big tax bills based on their companies' valuations, even before they've cashed out. Prop 40 includes provisions that would allow qualifying taxpayers with illiquid wealth to defer payments, but Rauh argues those protections are inadequate.
" You have to understand that the entire startup ecosystem of California is threatened by taxes like this," Rauh argues. He predicts that "investors will pull out of California if the wealth tax is passed."
Zucman hears echoes of an earlier fight in all these warnings about taxing wealth: the fight over taxing income back in the early 20th century. Back then, he says, critics argued that an income tax would drive people away and hurt the economy.
He points to Wisconsin's adoption of a progressive income tax in 1911 as a crucial turning point. Two years later, America adopted the federal income tax we know today. Zucman hopes California can play a similar role for taxing wealth.
"I have little doubt that it will work very well for the state of California," he says. "And then very quickly you'll see other states doing the same."
Ultimately, Zucman hopes this movement will lead to a federal wealth tax. He acknowledges that billionaires are less likely to move to avoid a national wealth tax than a state one.
Rauh also expects less flight under a national wealth tax. But he argues that such a tax would still discourage investment and threaten the U.S. economy.
California voters are now being deluged with ads and glossy mailers in what has proven to be one of the most expensive ballot fights in the state's history. If wealth tax supporters have their way, the rest of America could face a similar choice in the near future. For now, it's up to Californians to decide whether this wealth tax is a golden opportunity or a costly mistake.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. Should California tax billionaires? How McClatchy Editorial Board sees Props. 40, 41 & 42
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
October 27, 2026 11:24 AM
A float balloon featuring Mr. Monopoly was featured by San Diego demonstrators in 2021, an example of mounting frustration aimed at the wealthy. On the November election ballot in California, Proposition 40 seeks to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to fund healthcare in the state.
Rob Nikolewski
TNS
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is the most controversial proposition on the ballot. Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 seek to nullify Prop. 40. In the articles linked below, the journalists explain their positions.
Proposition 40: A one-time wealth tax tied to federal cuts
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of Californians worth more than $1 billion. Ninety percent of the proceeds would be reserved for healthcare; the remaining 10% would go to education, food assistance and tax administration.
The Bee’s endorsement (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html) is anchored to a specific fiscal threat. According to the California Budget & Policy Center, President Donald Trump’s federal budget bill — known as H.R. 1 — contains the largest cuts to healthcare and food assistance in U.S. history. The center estimates Medi-Cal cuts alone could cost California tens of billions of dollars and cause about 1.3 million Californians to lose healthcare access by 2030. KFF and the Commonwealth Fund have warned the federal cuts could force rural hospitals, community health centers and safety-net medical centers to shed workers and eliminate services, with those institutions standing to lose billions in revenue.
The revenue projections for Prop. 40 vary dramatically depending on who is modeling. Proponents predict about $100 billion. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office projects California would probably collect only tens of billions. Stanford economist Joshua Rauh and other Hoover Institution researchers estimate the tax would collect roughly $40 billion — but claim it would ultimately cost California $25 billion, because they believe billionaires will leave the state, taking future income and capital gains tax payments with them.
The LAO, by contrast, projects behavioral changes — including the possibility of billionaires leaving California to avoid the tax — would probably reduce future state revenues by less than $1 billion annually.
The editorial board acknowledges California’s dangerous reliance on volatile revenues from its wealthiest residents, and the endorsement was not unanimous. But a majority concluded that waiting for a perfect federal fix is untenable while coverage disappears. “Billionaires have every right to fight a tax that could cost them billions,” the board wrote. “But voters should recognize the enormous political power that such wealth can buy and ask why so much of that power has been exercised through campaign committees rather than direct public engagement.”
Prop. 40 will almost certainly face litigation, particularly over its provision applying the tax to billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026 — months before voters decide the measure. Courts have upheld many tax laws with retroactive provisions, but survival is not guaranteed. Proponents told the editorial board they anticipated litigation and built an accelerated judicial review process into the initiative itself.
The board’s conditional support comes with a demand: every Prop. 40 dollar should be publicly traceable through an online dashboard showing collection, allocation, which providers and programs received funds, and whether the spending actually preserved coverage, access and health outcomes. Lawmakers, the board argues, should use the breathing room to devise the permanent solution Prop. 40 cannot deliver.
Prop. 41: Transparency framing, nullification mechanics
Prop. 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) is marketed as a constitutional amendment adding transparency and accountability to ballot measures for special taxes — mandating audits for voter-approved special taxes and ongoing reviews every four years.
The editorial board calls this framing insidious. Prop. 41 is supported by Building a Better California, funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other CEOs and entrepreneurs. One of its most important provisions would ban taxes on or after Jan. 1, 2026, that are exempt from state spending limits — and Prop. 40, as written, is exempt from state spending limits.
That is the mechanism. If Prop. 41 collects more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, its provisions prevail under the California Constitution, and Prop. 40 is effectively voided.
“What’s insidious Prop. 41 is that it is presented as a good governance measure when it’s really about defeating Prop. 40,” the collective editorial boards wrote. The concern is asymmetric visibility: Prop. 40 has drawn significant attention, while Prop. 41 has not — exactly the dynamic a sophisticated nullification campaign would want.
The endorsement (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) urges a no vote.
Prop. 42: The 401(k) decoy
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html) is pitched as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts, barring new state taxes on those assets and restricting certain retroactive taxes. The editorial board describes it bluntly as a poison pill.
The suggestion that any governor would raid middle-class retirement accounts, the board writes, is implausible — any governor who tried “would soon be unemployed.” Even the Legislature, which the board characterizes as inclined to spend more than it should, “knows not to mess with your 401(k).” Opponents also note it appears to be an unsettled legal question whether retirement accounts can be taxed at all, because no government has tried.
Prop. 42 would embed its restrictions in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them. The board argues it would create “the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property” while in fact restricting the state’s future tax options — until the next constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure altered that policy.
The real function is familiar: if Prop. 42 collects more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, the wealth tax does not take effect.
“Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires,” the editorial board wrote. “Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.”
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

# Letters: Billionaires will end up paying much more than 5% under Prop 40’s tax
By Chronicle readersOct 1, 2026

Regarding “Katie Porter: Don’t be fooled by the California billionaire tax’s false progressive bravado” (Open Forum, SFChronicle.com, Sept. 21): The “one-time 5%” billionaire tax costs more than 5%.
The tax must be paid in cash.
For company founders whose wealth is mostly low-basis stock, that means selling shares and paying capital gains tax on the sale.
At top rates (20% federal, 3.8% net investment income tax and 13.3% California), about 37 cents of every dollar of gain goes to taxes.
For founders holding very low-basis stock, raising cash to pay a 5% wealth tax could require selling roughly 8% of their holdings under top-rate tax assumptions.
The measure’s installment, valuation and illiquidity provisions could add further costs, although the exact burden would vary substantially by taxpayer.
Spreading payments over five years doesn’t help much, because the measure imposes a nondeductible 7.5% annual deferral charge on the unpaid balance.
Article continues below this ad
Then come the valuation fights.
Private companies, foreign holdings and partnership interests have no market price, and years of litigation over them will add legal and appraisal costs on both sides.
A 5% rate is a slogan, not a price tag.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> There is a legitimate debate to be had about whether the wealthiest Californians should pay more in taxes. But Proposition 40 is the wrong tax, structured the wrong way, and would only make California’s budget problems worse.
Even voters who believe billionaires should contribute more should reject a measure that is so poorly drafted. Proposition 40 is ballot-box budgeting at its worst: a one-time tax that would raise tens of billions of dollars ostensibly for healthcare — but has insufficient guardrails to ensure the funds are spent to actually address Californians’ most pressing healthcare needs.
Instead, the funds could go to any interest group, including health insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies and for-profit hospitals. These sectors all play an important role in our healthcare system, but we should not allocate precious taxpayer dollars to subsidize these for-profit corporations.
Advertisement
Equally problematic: Proposition 40’s proponents excluded other key state priorities like education, public safety, housing, wildfire prevention and more. California is confronting persistent deficits, struggling public schools, a housing and homelessness crisis, rising costs for families, and growing demands for wildfire prevention, public safety and other essential services. Yet Proposition 40 provides little to nothing for these priorities.
Supporters describe Proposition 40 as a one-time solution to an immediate crisis. Californians have heard that before. Proposition 30 was sold as a temporary tax increase (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx) in 2012. Voters later extended (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016) much of it through 2030. Once government programs become dependent on a revenue source, “temporary” taxes have a way of becoming permanent political expectations.
The reality is that one-time taxes create a fiscal cliff, which leads to new and additional taxes when the money runs out. Even worse, this measure would drive out some of our state’s most successful residents, taking jobs, economic benefits and billions in tax revenue with them.
And Proposition 40 would establish an especially dangerous precedent. If one interest group can write a tax measure, target a politically unpopular group and dedicate the proceeds to its preferred programs, others will follow.
Advertisement
That is no way to govern a state with an economy larger than most countries.
California can ask the wealthy to contribute more without embracing a measure this flawed. Proposition 40 is a temporary tax masquerading as a fiscal solution, a permanent precedent for ballot-box budgeting and the wrong answer to the very real problems facing California.
Vote no on Proposition 40.

The editorial contends that Proposition 40 is the wrong kind of tax because it is a one-time levy on billionaires that is poorly drafted, invites ballot-box budgeting, and lacks adequate guardrails to ensure funds actually address Californians’ most urgent healthcare needs, rather than subsidizing for-profit insurers, drugmakers and hospitals.
The piece argues that by narrowly channeling revenue to healthcare interests, the measure largely ignores other core state priorities such as education, housing, homelessness, wildfire prevention and public safety, even as California wrestles with budget deficits and mounting pressures on schools, housing and essential services.
The editorial warns that labeling Proposition 40 as a “temporary” tax is misleading, pointing to past experience with short-term tax increases that were later extended, and asserts that one-time taxes create fiscal cliffs that trigger future demands for additional taxes rather than solving underlying budget problems.
The column contends that the measure risks pushing some of California’s wealthiest residents to leave the state, taking jobs, economic activity and substantial income-tax revenue with them, an argument echoed by critics who caution that a retroactive, one-time wealth tax could spook the ultra-wealthy and destabilize an already volatile budget [1] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-08/californias-billionaire-tax-measure-split-democratic-allies) [3] (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax) [8] (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) [12] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-30/labor-organizers-spearheading-california-billionaire-tax-rebuffed-by-parent-union) .
The article argues that Proposition 40 would set a dangerous precedent by allowing a single interest group to write a tax measure targeting a politically unpopular class of taxpayers and then dedicate the proceeds to its preferred programs, inviting copycat efforts and undermining responsible, comprehensive budgeting for an economy larger than that of many countries [5] (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/08/10/the-many-fronts-of-the-billionaire-tax-fight-01031349) [6] (https://garryslist.org/posts/a-primer-the-labor-and-public-interest-coalition-against-prop-40) .
The editorial’s skepticism is reinforced by civil-rights organizations and Democratic groups that have publicly opposed Proposition 40, with statements warning that the tax could worsen fiscal pressures and squeeze funding for other essential public services such as education, public safety and housing [2] (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/08/27/california-naacp-equality-california-sf-dems-oppose-prop-40s-billionaire-tax/189233/) [5] (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/08/10/the-many-fronts-of-the-billionaire-tax-fight-01

Endorsement: California isn’t a lab rat. Prop 40 treats us like one
There’s no denying the visceral satisfaction of a billionaire bloodletting. But will the measure’s wealth tax actually help the state?
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:42 p.m.
Taxation, like everything else in life, is an exercise in trade-offs.
How much public good can a tax extract before it passes the tipping point into harm?
As it relates to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php) on California’s November ballot, many believe you don’t have to look very hard to find where the cost-benefit needle falls.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on anyone whose total net worth is greater than $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, and who was a California resident on Jan. 1, 2026. After administrative costs, 90% of the revenue would go to public healthcare, while the other 10% would go to food assistance and education. The total collected could range from $28 billion to $100 billion — depending on whose math you believe. (California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the state will “probably” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) collect “tens of billions.”)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Whatever the total, there’s no denying that California billionaires — who by some counts control a combined $2 trillion (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) in wealth — can afford to shoulder it.
Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and a coauthor of Prop 40, called the measure a “rounding error” on the fortunes of California’s wealthiest.
For this mostly bloodless toll, Californians get relief from President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful” Medicaid cuts and radiate with satisfaction at sending a landmark message about wealth inequality.
Or so it would seem.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Is Prop 40 so flawlessly executed that California has nothing to lose if it passes?
Opposition from the California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood, California Medical Association, the NAACP, California Professional Firefighters and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California suggests not.
Let’s start with the healthcare organizations, which would effectively receive 90% of Prop 40’s funds. Why are they opposed?
Dustin Corcoran, CEO of the California Medical Association, said in an endorsement interview that there’s no guarantee Prop 40’s payload will arrive in time to backfill Trump’s cuts. The state has no existing system for assessing billionaire wealth, he said, and it will likely take years to develop one.
Corcoran cited his experience as a backer of Prop 56, which passed in 2016 and imposed a tax on vape products.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“It probably took the Franchise Tax Board 10 years of us beating them up because they couldn’t figure out how to get the tax right,” he said. “And that was a fairly straightforward thing to try and figure out.”
Even if the money does land, and that’s a big if, Corcoran argued that weak “anti-supplantation” protections in the measure will allow lawmakers to spend its revenue however they see fit — undermining one of Prop 40’s most powerful arguments, the urgency of the moment for healthcare.
University of Missouri School of Law Professor David Gamage, one of Prop 40’s coauthors, disputed these notions. He estimated that “75% of billionaire wealth is in publicly traded assets,” making much of it easy to track. And even if the measure does have supplantation holes, political pressure will prevent California politicians from treating Prop 40 revenue like a slush fund.
These vague assurances don’t persuade Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Healthcare organizations like hers, she said, use forward-looking budgets. They can’t commit to providing services if they can’t definitively rely on money coming in to pay for them.
Meanwhile, Prop 40 puts the money Hicks can count on in jeopardy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because California’s budget is overly dependent on income taxes — roughly half of which (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7)historically come from the ultra-wealthy top 1% of taxpayers.
Studying the impacts of Prop 40 “was an eye-opening experience for what California’s tax structure is and how the wealthy are a part of it,” Hicks said.
This gets at the real questions surrounding Prop 40 and why so many otherwise progressive organizations oppose the tax: Will billionaires leave the state if the measure passes, and will they take their companies with them?
“Good riddance” is the popular retort among online commentators.
But that attitude is childish and self-defeating. A recent case study explained why.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, left California in 2020, citing high taxes as one of his reasons. He took Tesla’s corporate headquarters with him to Texas the following year.
By some estimates, California lost an estimated $2.5 billion (https://www.businessinsider.com/why-did-elon-musk-move-texas-wealth-tax-capital-gains-2021-11) in capital gains revenue from one stock transaction in the first year of Musk’s move. In a state where 40% of state dollars are required by law to go to public education, that’s a $1 billion hole in California’s school budget from one man alone.
This answers why the formidable California Teachers Association — never one to shy away from a back-alley tax brawl — doesn’t support Prop 40.
Then there are the jobs.
Many Tesla workers stayed behind in California. But new Tesla jobs are now sprouting up across Texas, including nearly 10,000 for a proposed $10 billion solar cell factory (https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/09/18/teslas-10-1-billion-texas-solar-gigafactory-clears-key-tax-hurdle/).
You’ve heard the aphorism, “Keep your friends close and your enemies closer.” Here’s a real-world example of why.
Sending billionaires and the jobs and economic might that come with them to Texas or Florida does not help California. Nor does it help the prospects for building a more just society. It simply makes those red states more powerful.
So, will Prop 40 send billionaires fleeing?
A working paper from Stanford says yes, (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) and argues that exodus will result in a net tax revenue loss of nearly $39 billion for California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Indeed, some billionaires — most famously Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has dumped hundreds of millions into opposing Prop 40 — have already announced their departures.
Some economists dispute the Stanford study (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988796082176375), arguing it ignores basic human motivation. Prop 40 will hit any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. Why would they uproot their lives now over a one-time tax they have to pay regardless — especially one they can easily afford?
We’d counter that California’s nation-leading 13.3% marginal income tax rate — necessary as it may be (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php), given our state’s finances — already poses a flight risk. Even Gamage said he was “uncomfortable” (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) with the top rate. A wealth tax merely compounds a danger that already exists.
It’s true that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has committed to ponying up (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/billionaires-fight-tax-hike-jensen-160907521.html) his estimated $8 billion in dues. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has apparently agreed to stay in California for eight years after strong-arming the company (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php#:~:text=Meta%20revealed%20in%20a%20Securities%20and%20Exchange%20Commission%20filing%20that%20Mark%20Zuckerberg%20was%20considering%20leaving%20California%2C%20but%20agreed%20to%20stay%20after%20the%20company%20gave%20him%20a%20new%20stock%20deal) into eating his wealth tax burden.
Yet the debate around flight risk has largely focused on the wealthiest of the wealthy. Less discussed are the paper billionaires — those with unrealized stakes in valuable startups and other private companies.
Prop 40’s method for assessing this wealth (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan) is dubious. Some believe the measure allows voting shares or control percentage to be used in calculating wealth, rather than ownership stake, which could be wildly off. The measure does offer a mechanism for the wealthy to contest their asset valuations, but at what point are companies going to decide enough is enough and seek their fortunes elsewhere?
“Only idiot startup founders stay in Cali” if Prop 40 passes, billionaire investor Mark Cuban has said on social media. (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-17/mark-cuban-rips-ro-khannas-insane-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-plan?utm_source=chatgpt.com) “You can bet if I’m investing in a multi-billion-dollar startup, I’m asking them to move from California first.”
“Boo hoo,” you say?
California’s startup culture is a crucial engine of its economy. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, companies in the state receive nearly half of all American venture capital (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2024/4942/CalFacts-2024-120224.pdf). Another study found these investments help employ 1.2 million people (https://www.nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/California-VC-State-Data.pdf). As companies grow their roots, California’s budget sees the benefit.
Many argue that the talent ecosystem in California makes an exodus impossible.
But people said the same thing about Hollywood for decades. Now the entertainment industry is shedding thousands of jobs to states like Georgia and North Carolina that offer more favorable economic incentives.
If movie titans are willing to abandon a company town practically built to indulge their excess, it’s not a stretch to imagine a significant portion of the tech universe fleeing to Miami or Austin, where workforce housing is cheaper, they would pay no state income tax, and the sword of future wealth taxes would no longer hang over their endeavors.
All this speaks to why tackling extreme wealth is better approached at the federal level. There’s evidence from Spain and elsewhere that the wealthy will shop around regionally (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to) for lower taxes. There’s much less evidence that they’ll flee the country.
We are already seeing momentum for a federal inequality crackdown. Democrats are poised to retake Congress, and Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Burbank, recently announced legislation that would impose an excise tax of 23.8% (https://news.bgov.com/bloomberg-government-news/house-democrat-pitches-new-wealth-tax-as-midterms-draw-near) on most line-of-credit loans — which are leveraged against assets like stocks — above $1 million.
Ever wonder how the Zuckerbergs of the world get by on a salary of $1? Borrowing against stock gives them access to cash without having to pay capital gains. In fact, in some cases, interest payments on these loans are tax deductible under federal policy.
Fixing these loopholes would force the ultra-wealthy to either take salaries or liquidate assets when they need cash, which would mean income tax boons for states like California.
Obviously, with Trump still in charge, it could take a few years for these and other changes to manifest.
Instead of being patient, however, Prop 40 throws the full weight of risk on California’s shoulders now.
“Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?”
We wholeheartedly agree with these sentiments, espoused by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders at a recent rally in support of Prop 40.
But living up to them demands strategic thinking, not primal screaming.
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be.
Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tLQFHYqkVtY)
It just happens to be one dropped into the maw of the world’s fourth-largest economy — a wealthy state in aggregate, but one with a volatile, incoherent system of taxation (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php) and the highest poverty rate in the nation.
If Prop 40 backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. Our sales and income taxes are already the highest in the nation; there’s no more room for hikes. Meanwhile, Prop 13 stunts our ability to raise new revenue from property taxes.
No one is coming to save us. And it won’t be the wealthy who suffer.
Maybe, just maybe, the stakes are too high in California to be playing a game of chicken. Maybe the brightest and boldest minds in the field of economic justice should help stabilize California’s tax base before turning our state into a laboratory?
